one: Cohesion: things that change together live together. Coupling: how much one module must know about another. Aim for high cohesion, low coupling.
an: A good kitchen keeps all baking tools in one drawer (cohesion), and the baker does not need to know how the dishwasher works (low coupling).
how: Signs of tight coupling: changing one feature touches 15 files across folders; a module imports another's internals; shared mutable globals; long chains like order.customer.address.city.name.
Organise by feature/domain (checkout/, catalog/) rather than by technical type (components/, services/, utils/) when things change together by feature.
Depend on small, stable interfaces; hide details behind them.
why: It is the underlying principle behind almost every other design guideline: SOLID, modules, microservices, clean architecture.
trade: Over-decoupling (interfaces for everything, layers of indirection) makes code hard to follow. Decouple where change actually happens.

myth.m: DRY everything: any duplicated code should be shared.
myth.r: Sharing code couples its users. Two similar pieces that change for different reasons should often stay separate. Duplication is cheaper than the wrong abstraction.

q.s: A shared formatPrice util is used by checkout and admin reports. Checkout needs rounding changed; reports must not change. What does this reveal?
o: Need more utils
The two uses only looked the same; they change for different reasons and should be separate
Use a class
Write more tests only
q.e: Shared code should represent one concept with one reason to change.

more: Connascence as a finer vocabulary for coupling
The rule of three before abstracting
lab: Pick a recent feature you built. List every file you touched. Group them by folder. If they span many folders, sketch a feature-folder layout that would have kept the change local.

plain:
Coupling is how much one part of your code depends on the details of another. Cohesion is how well the things inside one part belong together. Good code has high cohesion (related things together) and low coupling (parts know little about each other).

The practical test: when you change one feature, how many unrelated files do you have to touch?
bridge: A component that reaches into a global store, reads five nested fields and calls three services is tightly coupled. A component that receives the two props it needs is loosely coupled.

walk.title: When sharing code creates coupling
steps: Checkout and admin reports both format prices, so someone creates a shared formatPrice().
Checkout needs a change: show prices rounded to the nearest 1,000 so'm.
Changing formatPrice() would also change the reports, where accountants need exact amounts.
The two uses looked the same but had different reasons to change. Sharing them coupled two unrelated features.
Fix: separate functions (formatCheckoutPrice, formatAccountingAmount). A little duplication, much less coupling.

terms: Dependence between parts of the code.
How closely the contents of one part belong together.
Don't Repeat Yourself; useful, but not at the cost of wrong coupling.
Organising code by feature instead of by file type.
insights: Git history is the best coupling detector: files that keep changing in the same commits belong together, wherever they live today.
The expensive coupling is the hidden kind: shared database tables, shared config keys, “call init() first” rules. An import graph does not show it.
Coupling to something stable (the standard library, a versioned public API) is cheap. Coupling to code that changes every week is what hurts.

prod.summary: In a real codebase, coupling shows up as change cost: how many files, teams and deploys one feature needs. Seniors read it from git history and import graphs, not from opinions, and they enforce the important boundaries with a tool so they do not erode one PR at a time.
checklist: Does this PR touch many folders for one feature? A feature that edits 4+ unrelated modules is a sign the boundary is in the wrong place.
Does any module import another module's internals (../billing/internal/...) instead of its public index.ts? Block deep imports with ESLint no-restricted-imports or dependency-cruiser.
Are there import cycles? Run madge --circular src or dependency-cruiser in CI; cycles make load order and refactors fragile.
Is a new “shared” util used by two features that change for different reasons? Prefer two small functions over one function with flags.
Do two services read and write the same database tables? That is hidden coupling: a column rename breaks a service whose code you never touched.
Is there temporal coupling (call init() before run())? Make the wrong order impossible, e.g. return the ready object from the constructor or factory.
Are changes that always ship together (files with high co-change in git) living in the same module?
numbers: ESLint complexity rule warns when cyclomatic complexity passes 20 by default; many teams lower it to 10–15.
Sandi Metz's rule of thumb (2016): “duplication is far cheaper than the wrong abstraction”. Many teams wait for a third copy before extracting (the rule of three).
failures: A one-line change to a shared utils/date.ts breaks the invoice PDF, the mobile API and a nightly job.

One “shared” helper had several unrelated callers with different needs. Fix: give each feature its own function, or move the helper into the one feature that owns it; keep truly shared code small and stable.
Service B starts failing after Service A renames a column in “its own” table.
Both services share a database, so the schema is a hidden public API. Fix: one owner per table; others read through an API, an event, or a read-only view with a stable contract.
ReferenceError: Cannot access 'X' before initialization appears after an innocent import was added.
An import cycle (A imports B imports A) changed module load order. Fix: break the cycle by moving the shared type to a third module; add madge --circular to CI.
Every feature PR needs reviews from 3 teams and takes a week to merge.
Code is organised by layer (controllers/, services/), so every feature crosses team folders. Fix: organise by feature/domain with clear owners (CODEOWNERS per feature folder).

code.title: Enforcing module boundaries with dependency-cruiser
code.note: $1 refers back to the feature captured in from, so a feature can import its own files freely but only another feature's index.ts.

qs.s: Git history shows that orders/OrderForm.tsx, api/orderController.ts, services/orderService.ts and db/orderRepo.ts change together in 90% of commits, but four different teams own those folders. What is the best structural change?
o: Add an interface between each layer so the teams can work independently
Write more integration tests across the four folders
Move them into one features/orders/ module owned by one team
Merge all four files into one large file
qs.e: Things that change together should live together (high cohesion). Extra interfaces add indirection but the files still change together, so the coordination cost stays. Merging into one file mixes concerns; a feature folder keeps separate files with one owner.

qs.s: Two services, Orders and Reports, both query the orders table directly. The Orders team wants to split total into subtotal and tax. What is the real risk and the long-term fix?
o: Reports breaks silently because the table is a hidden contract; give the table one owner and expose data to Reports via an API, event or stable view
No risk, because both services use the same ORM
Only a performance risk; add an index
The migration will lock the table; run it at night
qs.e: A shared database couples the services through the schema. The ORM does not help: Reports' queries still name the old column. Locking may matter, but it is not the coupling problem.

qs.s: A reviewer sees if (user.account.plan.limits.seats > team.members.length) repeated in 9 components. What is the coupling problem and the smallest good fix?
o: Nothing; optional chaining would make it safe
Move it into a global Redux selector used everywhere
Use a class hierarchy for plans
Every component knows the internal shape of plan data; add one function such as canAddSeat(user, team) next to the plan model and call it
qs.e: Long property chains spread knowledge of a structure (Law of Demeter). If limits moves, 9 files break. One domain function hides the shape. Optional chaining hides the crash, not the coupling; a global selector still exposes the structure.

qs.s: The app runs as native ES modules on Node 22 ("type": "module"), compiled by tsc with module: nodenext, and main.ts starts with import './orders/index.js'. Read the two modules. What happens at startup?

code.title: orders/index.ts and pricing/index.ts

o: It works: ES modules hoist all exports, so ORDER_STATUSES is ready before pricing runs
Nothing fails at startup; PAYABLE is just an empty set until the first order
ReferenceError: Cannot access 'ORDER_STATUSES' before initialization, because pricing runs before orders has finished; move the constant into a third module that both import
The bundler refuses to build because circular imports are illegal in ES modules
qs.e: orders starts loading, imports pricing, and pricing runs its top-level code while orders is still unfinished. The binding exists but is in the “temporal dead zone”, so reading it throws. Hoisting creates the binding, not the value. Cycles are legal, which is why they are dangerous: they fail only when load order changes. (If the code were compiled to CommonJS, the value would silently be undefined and PAYABLE would be empty, which is even worse.)

qs.s: Six services depend on an internal package @acme/common. It holds date helpers, a logger wrapper and the full Order type. Every change to Order forces a release of all six services in the same week. What is the best long-term change?
o: Keep only small, stable, generic code in the shared package; give Order back to the service that owns it and let others use its API schema or a generated client, versioned separately
Add more tests to @acme/common so changes are safer
Move to a monorepo that rebuilds and redeploys all six services on every change
Copy the whole package into each service
qs.e: A domain type shared as a library makes every consumer change when the owner changes. Generic helpers change rarely, so sharing them is cheap. A monorepo that redeploys everything makes the coupling faster to live with, but the six services are still forced to move together. Copying everything removes the coupling, but also the useful sharing of stable code.

qs.s: CI runs dependency-cruiser and prints this. Which fix solves both errors without hiding the problem?

code.title: depcruise output
code.src:
error no-deep-imports-between-features: src/features/checkout/ui/CartSummary.tsx → src/features/catalog/model/price.ts
  error no-circular: src/features/catalog/index.ts →
      src/features/checkout/index.ts →
      src/features/catalog/index.ts

x 2 dependency violations (2 errors, 0 warnings). 412 modules, 980 dependencies cruised.

o: Import price.ts through a path alias like @catalog/model/price so the rule no longer matches
Add a pathNot exception for catalog/model in the rule
Merge catalog and checkout into one feature folder

Export what checkout needs from catalog/index.ts, and break the cycle by moving the shared piece (for example the Price type) into a lower module both can import, or by making one side depend on the other only through an event or callback
qs.e: The first error says checkout reaches into catalog's internals; the public index.ts is the fix. The second says the two features depend on each other, so neither can change or load alone; one direction must go. An alias only changes the spelling of the same dependency, and an exception switches the alarm off. Merging can be right if the two really are one feature, but it is not the default answer to a single cycle.

qs.s: Robert C. Martin's instability metric is I = Ce / (Ca + Ce), where Ce = outgoing dependencies and Ca = incoming ones. money has Ca = 14, Ce = 1. flags-client has Ca = 2, Ce = 8. A PR makes money import flags-client. What is the instability of flags-client, and is this dependency a problem?
o: I = 0.2; fine, because flags-client is stable
I = 0.8; yes: a very stable module that 14 others rely on now depends on a volatile one, so flags-client changes can ripple into all 14. Pass the flag value into money instead
I = 0.8; fine, because only cycles matter, not direction
I = 0.25; fine, because flags-client has only 2 users
qs.e: 8 / (2 + 8) = 0.8, so flags-client is unstable: it depends on many things and will change often. The Stable Dependencies Principle says to depend toward stability. money (I = 1/15, about 0.07) is the base of 14 modules; giving it a volatile dependency spreads that volatility. Cycles are the worst case, but direction matters even without a cycle.

interview.q: You join a team with a large codebase. How do you find where coupling actually hurts, before proposing any refactor?
answer: Use git history: which files change together (co-change), and which PRs touch many folders or need several teams to review. That is the real cost of coupling.
Draw the import graph with dependency-cruiser or madge; look for cycles and for features that import other features' internals.
Look for hidden coupling that imports do not show: shared database tables, shared config keys, events with no owner, temporal coupling (“call init first”).
Rank by pain: high churn plus many incidents first; ugly but stable areas last.
Propose small, enforced boundaries (public index.ts, a CI rule) instead of a big restructure, and measure files-per-feature-PR before and after.
followups: How would you stop the boundaries from eroding again after the refactor?
What would you do if two teams both claim ownership of the same module?

interview.q: When is duplication better than a shared abstraction? Give an example.
answer: When the two copies look the same today but change for different reasons or for different people (checkout price display vs accounting amounts).
A shared function couples its callers: every change needs to consider all of them, and it tends to grow flags and parameters.
Rule of three: wait until you see the third real case and understand what actually varies before extracting.
Sharing is right for things that have one meaning everywhere and change rarely: a Money type, date parsing, an HTTP client wrapper.
If a shared abstraction already went wrong, inline it back into callers first, then re-extract what is really common (Sandi Metz's advice).
followups: How do you spot a “wrong abstraction” in code review?
Does this advice change for microservices that share a library?

interview.q: Two services read and write the same Postgres tables. How do you decouple them without downtime?
answer: Pick one owner for each table; the owner is the only service allowed to write it.
Inventory what the other service actually reads and writes (query logs, pg_stat_statements, code search).
Give it a stable interface instead: an API, events (with an outbox), or a read-only view whose columns are a contract.
Move the other service onto that interface step by step behind a flag, then remove its grants on the table so it cannot drift back.
Only after that change the schema freely, using expand/contract for anything the interface still exposes.
Trade-off: an API adds latency and a network failure mode; for reporting, a replicated read model may be cheaper.
followups: What if the second service needs joins across both services' data for reports?
How do you handle a write that must update both services' data?

videos.t: SOLID Principles? Nope, just Coupling and Cohesion
videos.why: Argues SOLID reduces to coupling and cohesion.

one: Five object-oriented design guidelines about responsibilities and dependencies. Useful as vocabulary; apply with judgement.
an: Kitchen rules: one job per station, add new dishes without rebuilding stations, substitute chefs who follow the same recipe, small specific order slips, and stations depend on the menu rather than on a specific supplier.
how: Single responsibility: one reason to change. Open/closed: extend behaviour without editing stable code (e.g. new payment provider = new class implementing an interface).
Liskov substitution: a subtype must work wherever the parent type is expected, without surprises.
Interface segregation: small focused interfaces instead of one giant one. Dependency inversion: high-level logic depends on abstractions (PaymentGateway), not concrete details (StripeClient).
In functional and React code the same ideas appear as small components, composition over inheritance, and passing dependencies as props/arguments.
why: Interviewers use it to check design thinking, and it gives names to common smells in code review.
trade: Applied dogmatically it produces abstract factories and one-method interfaces everywhere. Use it to explain a problem you have, not to pre-empt imagined ones.

myth.m: SOLID is only for Java-style OOP.
myth.r: The principles are about change and dependencies; they map onto modules and functions in any language.

q.s: Adding a new payment provider requires editing a 600-line switch statement in checkout. Which principle is being violated most directly?
o: Liskov
Open/closed (and dependency inversion)
Interface segregation
None
q.e: Define a PaymentProvider interface; each provider implements it; checkout depends on the interface.

more: SOLID in functional and React code
Liskov violations in real code (e.g. read-only subclasses)
lab: Find a long switch on a type in your code. Refactor it into a map of strategy objects implementing one interface. Compare readability honestly; keep whichever is clearer.

plain:
SOLID is five guidelines for structuring code so it is easy to change. In short: give each part one job; add new behaviour by adding code rather than editing stable code; make substitutes behave like what they replace; keep interfaces small; depend on abstractions, not specific implementations.

They are useful vocabulary. Apply them when they solve a real problem, not everywhere.
bridge: In React terms: small components with one job (S), composition through props and children instead of editing a component for every new case (O), and passing dependencies in as props or hooks instead of importing a concrete service deep inside (D).

walk.title: Adding a new payment provider
steps: Today: a 600-line checkout() with if (provider === 'payme') {...} else if (provider === 'click') {...}.
Adding Octo means editing this function again, risking breaking the others.
Define an interface: PaymentProvider { createPayment(order): Promise<PaymentResult> }.
Each provider is its own small class/module implementing it. Checkout receives a provider and calls createPayment.
Adding Octo = writing one new module. Checkout does not change (open/closed), and it depends on the interface, not on Payme (dependency inversion).

terms: One reason to change per module.
Subtypes work anywhere the parent type works.
insights: Single responsibility is about reasons to change, not line counts. Code that two teams edit for two different reasons should be split, even if it is short.
Most of SOLID is about managing dependencies; that is the part worth remembering.
In interviews, explain a principle with a real example from your code, not a definition.

prod.summary: In production code SOLID mostly shows up in two places: integrations (payments, SMS, storage) where you want new providers without touching checkout, and large classes that every PR edits. Seniors use the principles to name a concrete smell in review, not as a checklist to apply everywhere.
checklist: Does this class or module have more than one reason to change (e.g. pricing rules AND email formatting AND SQL)? If yes, split along those reasons.
Does adding a new variant (provider, plan, file type) require editing a long switch in several places? Replace with one interface plus a registry.
Does any subclass throw NotImplemented or silently ignore a method of its parent? That is a Liskov violation; callers will break.
Do clients depend on methods they never call (a 30-method UserService injected for one lookup)? Split the interface by client need.
Does business logic import a concrete SDK (stripe, pg) directly? Put an interface owned by the business layer in between.
Is a new interface justified by a second real implementation (or a test fake)? An interface with one implementation and no tests is just extra indirection.
numbers: Robert C. Martin collected the principles around 2000; Michael Feathers coined the acronym “SOLID” around 2004.
The Liskov substitution principle comes from Barbara Liskov's 1987 keynote “Data Abstraction and Hierarchy” (formalised with Jeannette Wing in 1994).
failures: Adding the Octo payment provider broke Payme refunds in production.
All providers lived in one 600-line switch, and the edit changed a shared branch. Fix (open/closed + DI): one PaymentProvider interface, one module per provider, a registry keyed by provider name.
Error: ReadOnlyCache.set is not supported thrown deep inside a request.

A subclass that cannot do what its parent promises was passed where the parent was expected (Liskov violation). Fix: split the interface into CacheReader and CacheWriter and type callers by what they need.
A 3,000-line OrderService causes merge conflicts in nearly every PR.
Many reasons to change in one class (single responsibility violation). Fix: split by use case (PlaceOrder, RefundOrder, OrderReports), one small step per PR.
Codebase has 200 interfaces, each with exactly one implementation, and new devs cannot find where logic lives.
SOLID applied dogmatically. Fix: inline interfaces that have one implementation and no test fake; keep them only at real boundaries (I/O, vendors).

code.title: Open/closed with a provider registry
code.note: Checkout never changes when a provider is added (open/closed), and it depends on PaymentProvider, not on any SDK (dependency inversion).

qs.s: class Square extends Rectangle overrides setWidth to also set the height. A layout function calls r.setWidth(10); r.setHeight(5) and expects area 50, but gets 25 for squares. Which principle is broken and what is the fix?
o: Single responsibility; split Rectangle into two classes
Interface segregation; give Square fewer methods
Open/closed; make Rectangle final
Liskov substitution; Square cannot honour Rectangle's contract, so do not make it a subtype (use separate immutable shapes)
qs.e: Callers of Rectangle rely on width and height being independent. Square breaks that promise, so it is not a safe substitute. This is the classic Liskov example; the other principles do not describe the broken expectation.

qs.s: A ReportService class builds SQL, calculates tax totals, renders a PDF and emails it. A teammate wants to add an interface for each method. What is the most useful SOLID-based advice?
o: Add the interfaces; more interfaces always lower coupling
Split by reason to change: tax rules, PDF layout and delivery change for different people at different times, so they become separate modules
Leave it; SOLID only matters in Java
Convert it to static functions
qs.e: The problem is several reasons to change in one place (single responsibility). Interfaces on the same big class do not fix that. Static functions change the syntax, not the design.

qs.s: Your team wants to add a Logger interface in front of pino. There is one implementation, and tests already silence logs with pino({ level: 'silent' }). Is the interface worth it now?
o: Probably not yet: there is no second implementation and tests do not need one; add it when a real need (second backend, vendor lock-in risk) appears
Yes, dependency inversion requires an interface for every library
Yes, because interfaces make code faster
No, logging should use console.log instead
qs.e: Dependency inversion pays off where implementations really vary or where tests need a fake. An abstraction with no second user is cost without benefit; it can be added later in a small refactor.

qs.s: Developers run the app locally with LocalDiskStorage; production uses S3Storage. In dev, the profile page crashes with “not supported locally”. Which principle is broken, and what is the best fix?

code.title: storage.ts

o: Single responsibility: split LocalDiskStorage into two classes
Liskov substitution: it claims to be a Storage but breaks its promise; make url() work (for example, serve the folder from a dev static route)
Interface segregation: delete url() from Storage so no class has to implement it
Open/closed: S3Storage should be extended instead of implemented
qs.e: Callers rely on every Storage giving a URL. A substitute that throws is not a real substitute, which is exactly Liskov. Splitting the interface is right only when some callers truly do not need URLs; deleting url() here just moves the crash, because the profile page still needs a URL. TypeScript accepted the class, which shows that types check signatures, not behaviour.

qs.s: UserCard takes user: User (40 fields) but shows only the name and avatar. Tests must build a full User, and the card is used for team members who are not User objects. What is the smallest good change?
o: Make all 40 User fields optional
Pass only userId and fetch the user inside the card
Wrap the card in React.memo
Accept only what it uses: { name: string; avatarUrl: string } (or Pick<User, 'name' | 'avatarUrl'>)
qs.e: This is interface segregation at component level: depend on the small shape you use. Making fields optional weakens types for every other user of User. Fetching inside the card couples a display component to the data layer and adds a request per card. memo is about re-renders, not dependencies.

qs.s: A teammate says: “This follows dependency inversion, because db is passed in as a parameter.” Is that right?

code.title: billing/core/issueInvoice.ts

o: No. It is dependency injection, but the core still depends on a concrete detail (Prisma's client and types). Inversion means the core owns a small interface such as InvoiceStore, and a Prisma adapter implements it
Yes. Any dependency passed as a parameter satisfies dependency inversion
Yes, because PrismaClient is a class, and classes are abstractions
No, because dependency inversion requires a DI container
qs.e: Injection is about how a dependency arrives; inversion is about who owns the abstraction. Here the core must still import Prisma, and tests must fake Prisma's huge API. With an interface owned by the core, the source-code dependency points from the adapter to the core. A container is never required.

qs.s: The app supports one country and one tax rule that changes about once a year. A developer proposes a plugin system: a TaxStrategy interface, a registry and a factory, “so it is open/closed”. What is the best review response?
o: Approve: open/closed should be applied from the start
Ask for an abstract factory as well, for future countries
Keep one well-tested calculateTax() function; introduce the strategy interface when a second real rule set (a second country) arrives
Move the tax rule into a database table so it can change without deploys
qs.e: Open/closed pays off where variation actually happens. With one rule that changes yearly, a plain function is easier to read and to change, and extracting a strategy later is a small refactor. A database table looks flexible but moves logic out of code review and tests.

interview.q: Which SOLID principle do you find most useful in practice, and where have you seen SOLID make code worse?
answer: Most useful is usually dependency inversion at I/O boundaries: payments, SMS, storage behind interfaces the core owns. It makes tests fast and vendors replaceable.
Single responsibility helps in review: “this class changes for pricing reasons and for email reasons” is a concrete argument for a split.
Made worse: interfaces with exactly one implementation and no test fake, factories for objects that never vary, tiny classes that hide the flow across 10 files.
A good answer gives a real example with the before and after, and the cost (more files, more indirection) as well as the benefit.
The rule: apply a principle to fix a pain you can name, not in advance.
followups: How would you undo over-abstraction in an existing codebase?
How do these principles apply to React components?

interview.q: What is the difference between dependency injection and dependency inversion?
answer: Dependency injection is a technique: a component receives its dependencies from outside (constructor, parameter, props) instead of creating them.
Dependency inversion is a design rule: high-level policy should not depend on low-level details; both depend on an abstraction owned by the policy side.
You can inject a concrete class (DI without inversion), and you can have an interface but still create the implementation inside (inversion without DI).
Together: the core defines PaymentGateway, a Stripe adapter implements it, and the composition root injects the adapter.
Test: does the core's import list contain any vendor or framework package? If yes, it is not inverted.
followups: Where should the interface file live, and why does that matter?
Is a DI container needed for either?

interview.q: Give an example of a Liskov substitution violation you have seen, ideally in TypeScript or frontend code.
answer: A subclass or implementation that throws “not supported” for a method of its interface (read-only cache, local storage without URLs).
A subtype that requires more than the parent (stricter input checks) or promises less (may return null where the parent never does).
A wrapper component that accepts a base component's props but silently ignores some, like disabled, so callers' expectations break.
TypeScript checks shapes, not behaviour, so these violations compile; they are caught by shared contract tests that every implementation must pass.
Fix by splitting the interface by capability, or by not using inheritance where the “is-a” promise is not real.
followups: How would you write one test suite that every implementation of an interface must pass?
Why is the Square/Rectangle example about mutability?

videos.t: SOLID Principles: Do You Really Understand Them?
videos.why: Each SOLID principle with a short code example.

one: Passing a component the things it depends on, rather than letting it create or import them itself.
an: A chef who is handed ingredients can cook with farm produce in the restaurant and plastic props in a photo shoot. A chef who grows their own vegetables cannot.
how: Instead of class OrderService { db = new PostgresDb() }, use constructor(private db: Db). Production passes Postgres; tests pass an in-memory fake.
DI containers (Angular, NestJS, Spring, .NET) wire dependencies automatically from type declarations and scopes (singleton, per request).
In React: props, context and hooks are lightweight DI. In plain functions: pass dependencies as parameters.
why: Testability, swappable implementations, and explicit dependencies you can see in the signature.
trade: Containers add magic: harder to see where something comes from. Plain constructor or parameter injection is enough for most code.

myth.r: Passing an argument is dependency injection. Frameworks automate the wiring.

q.s: A function calls Date.now() and fetch() directly, so tests are flaky and slow. DI-style fix?
o: Mock the global object in every test
Pass a clock and an HTTP client as parameters (with defaults) so tests can inject fakes
Delete the tests
Use setTimeout
q.e: Explicit dependencies make behaviour deterministic under test.

plain:
Dependency injection means a piece of code receives the things it depends on (database, HTTP client, clock) from outside, instead of creating or importing them itself.

Then you can give it real ones in production and fake ones in tests, and you can see its dependencies in its signature.
bridge: Passing a function as a prop instead of importing it inside the component is dependency injection. React Context is a form of it too. Angular and NestJS have it built in.

walk.title: Making a function testable
steps: Before: async function isTrialExpired(userId) { const user = await db.users.find(userId); return Date.now() > user.trialEnds }.
Testing it needs a real database and depends on the current time; the test changes result over time.
After: function isTrialExpired(user, now) { return now > user.trialEnds }. The caller loads the user and passes the time.
Test: isTrialExpired({ trialEnds: 100 }, 200) === true. No database, no flakiness, runs in a millisecond.
Production code passes Date.now(); tests pass any time they want.

terms: Something your code needs to work (DB, API client, clock).
Passing a dependency in from outside.
A simple working stand-in used in tests.
A framework that wires dependencies automatically.
insights: DI moves the question “which implementation?” to one place at startup. That single place is what makes swapping and testing cheap.
Time and randomness are dependencies too; inject them for deterministic tests.
Hidden imports of global singletons make code hard to test and hard to change.

prod.summary: In production DI decides two things: which instance of a dependency each request gets (scope) and where all the wiring lives (the composition root). Most real DI bugs are scope bugs: per-request data stored in a singleton, or a request-scoped provider making a whole controller tree slow.
checklist: Is there exactly one composition root (e.g. main.ts or the framework module) where real implementations are chosen? new PostgresDb() inside business code is a smell.
Is any per-request data (current user, tenant ID, locale) stored on a singleton? Use request scope, AsyncLocalStorage, or pass it as an argument.
Are time, randomness and IDs injected (clock, idGenerator) so tests are deterministic?
Are long-lived clients (DB pool, Redis, HTTP agent) created once and shared? Creating a pool per request exhausts connections.
Does code pull dependencies from a global container (container.get(X)) in the middle of logic? That is the service locator anti-pattern; inject through the constructor.
Can you read a class's dependencies from its constructor alone? If it has 8+ dependencies, it probably does too much.
numbers: NestJS: the default provider scope is singleton; REQUEST scope “bubbles up”, so a controller that depends on a request-scoped provider becomes request-scoped too (a new instance per request).
Angular: @Injectable({ providedIn: 'root' }) creates one app-wide instance, and the service is tree-shaken if nothing injects it.
failures: User A sometimes sees User B's data under load; impossible to reproduce locally.

A singleton service stored this.currentUser per request, and concurrent requests overwrote it. Fix: pass the user as an argument or use AsyncLocalStorage/request scope; never put request state on singletons.
Postgres logs FATAL: sorry, too many clients already after a deploy.
A new Pool() was created inside a transient or request-scoped provider, so every request opened new connections. Fix: create the pool once in the composition root as a singleton and inject it.
p99 latency rises after one provider was marked Scope.REQUEST.
Request scope bubbled up and the whole controller chain is now constructed per request. Fix: keep providers singleton and pass request data explicitly, or use durable providers / AsyncLocalStorage.
NestJS fails at startup: Nest can't resolve dependencies of the OrderService (?).

The injected class is not provided in the module's scope, or there is a circular import that makes the type undefined at decoration time. Fix: export/import the provider in the right module; break the cycle (do not reach for forwardRef first).

code.title: Plain constructor DI with a composition root
code.note: No framework needed. The pool is created once in main.ts; the test injects a fixed clock, so it gives the same result on every day it runs.

qs.s: In a NestJS app, AuditService (singleton) stores this.userId = req.user.id in a middleware and reads it later when writing audit rows. Under load, some audit rows have the wrong user. Best fix?
o: Pass the user ID explicitly (or read it from AsyncLocalStorage) instead of storing it on a shared singleton
Make the database column nullable
Add a mutex around the audit write
Increase the Node.js thread pool size
qs.e: A singleton is shared by all concurrent requests, so the field is overwritten between the middleware and the write. A mutex would serialise the whole app. The thread pool is unrelated; JavaScript code runs on one thread and the interleaving happens at await points.

qs.s: Code review finds this inside a use case: const mailer = container.get(Mailer); mailer.send(...). Tests have to set up the global container. What is the issue?
o: Nothing; this is the recommended DI style
It is slower than constructor injection
It is the service locator anti-pattern: the dependency is hidden from the signature; inject Mailer through the constructor instead
The mailer should be a static class
qs.e: A service locator hides what the class needs, so you only find out at runtime or by reading every line. Constructor injection makes dependencies visible and easy to fake. Speed is not the real concern.

qs.s: A team uses manual constructor injection in a 40-service Express app. main.ts now has 150 lines of new X(new Y(...)). Which response is most reasonable?
o: Go back to importing singletons directly inside each module
That is acceptable; split the composition root by feature (one createOrdersModule(deps) per feature), and consider a container only if the wiring keeps hurting
Make every service a global variable
Switch the whole app to Angular for its DI
qs.e: A long composition root is the honest cost of explicit wiring and is easy to organise by feature. Hidden imports bring back the testability problems DI solved. A container is an option, not a requirement.

qs.s: In this NestJS app, TenantContext is request-scoped. What happens to ReportsService and ReportsController?

code.title: reports.module.ts (excerpt)

o: Nest throws at startup, because a singleton cannot depend on a request-scoped provider
ReportsService stays a singleton and keeps the first request's tenant forever
TenantContext is quietly turned into a singleton
Both become request-scoped (scope bubbles up), so Nest creates new instances on every request: more work per request, and the cache map is empty every time
qs.e: NestJS documents that request scope bubbles up the injection chain. Nothing crashes, which is why it surprises people: latency rises, and in-memory state on the service no longer survives between requests. Some other containers do throw for this (or capture the first instance, a “captive dependency”), which makes the first two options tempting.

qs.s: This handler serves about 60 requests per second against Postgres with the default max_connections = 100. node-postgres closes idle clients after idleTimeoutMillis (default 10,000 ms). Roughly what happens?

code.title: orders.ts

o: Nothing bad: pools are cheap, and each one closes when the request ends

Each request creates a new pool that opens its own connection, and that connection stays idle for about 10 s. That would need about 60 × 10 = 600 connections, far above 100, so within about 2 seconds Postgres starts refusing logins: FATAL: remaining connection slots are reserved for roles with the SUPERUSER attribute
Node runs out of memory first, long before Postgres complains
At most 10 connections are ever open, because max: 10 limits them
qs.e: max limits one pool, but every request makes a new pool. The pool is never ended, so its client lives until the idle timeout. Three of the 100 slots are reserved for superusers (superuser_reserved_connections = 3), so a normal app role is refused at 97 connections; sorry, too many clients already appears only when all 100 are taken. The fix is DI with the right lifetime: create one pool in the composition root and inject it. The “at most 10” answer is the common misreading.

qs.s: You want the request ID in every log line, including logs from code 12 calls deep. The value is not business data. Which approach fits best in a Node service?
o: A module-level variable currentRequestId set by middleware
Make every service request-scoped in the DI container
AsyncLocalStorage: middleware calls als.run({ requestId }, next), and the logger reads als.getStore()
Add a requestId parameter to every function on the path
qs.e: AsyncLocalStorage keeps a value per async call chain, so concurrent requests do not overwrite each other, unlike a module variable. Request scope everywhere costs instances on every request. Passing it explicitly is correct and is the better choice for business data like the current user, but for a cross-cutting value like log correlation it adds noise to every signature.

qs.s: After a deploy, expired tokens are accepted until the service restarts. Read the code. What is the bug?

code.title: tokens.ts

o: The clock is injected as a value, not as a function. now is read once when the service is created at startup; inject now: () => number = Date.now and call now() on each check
Date.now() returns seconds, so multiplying exp by 1000 is wrong
Nothing; default parameters are evaluated on every call, so now is always fresh
The service should be a class with a static method
qs.e: Default parameters are evaluated per call, but makeTokenService is called only once, at startup. So the “clock” is frozen at boot time. Date.now() returns milliseconds and JWT exp is in seconds, so the multiplication is correct. Inject time as a function so tests can fix it and production stays live.

interview.q: How do you wire dependencies in a Node/TypeScript backend without a DI framework, and when would you add one?
answer: Constructor or parameter injection everywhere; only the composition root (main.ts) creates real implementations.
Long-lived resources (DB pool, Redis client, HTTP agent) are created once there and passed down; request data is passed as arguments or through AsyncLocalStorage.
Split the root by feature (createOrdersModule(deps)) when it grows, so wiring stays readable.
Add a container when wiring is genuinely painful (hundreds of services, several scopes) or the framework already has one (NestJS, Angular).
Trade-off: a container removes boilerplate but hides where things come from and moves wiring errors from compile time to startup.
followups: How do you close resources cleanly on shutdown (SIGTERM)?
How do you test the composition root itself?

interview.q: What is the service locator pattern, and why do many people call it an anti-pattern?
answer: Code asks a global registry for what it needs (container.get(Mailer)) in the middle of its logic.
Dependencies are hidden: the constructor does not tell you what the class needs, so you find out at runtime.
Tests must configure global state, which leaks between tests and blocks parallel runs.
Constructor injection makes dependencies visible and fakes trivial.
Acceptable places: inside the composition root or framework glue code, where resolving is the whole job.
followups: Is React Context a service locator?
How would you migrate a codebase away from a locator step by step?

interview.q: What DI lifetime (scope) bugs have you seen, and how do you detect them?
answer: Per-request data stored on a singleton: users see each other's data under concurrency. Detect with concurrent integration tests and code review of fields on singletons.
Expensive resources created with a short lifetime (a pool per request): connection errors like too many clients already.
Captive dependency: a singleton holds a shorter-lived object, so it keeps stale state. Some containers detect this at startup; others do not.
Request scope bubbling up (NestJS): the whole controller chain is rebuilt per request and latency rises.
Prevention: default to singletons with no mutable request state, pass request data explicitly, and watch connection counts and p99 latency after DI changes.
followups: How would you reproduce a cross-request data leak locally?
Where would you put a per-tenant DB connection?

one: Named, reusable solutions to recurring design problems. A handful show up constantly in full-stack work.
an: Standard chess openings. You do not invent a new one each game; you recognise the position and apply a known plan.
how: Strategy: swap algorithms behind one interface (payment providers, pricing rules). Adapter: wrap a third-party API in your own interface. Facade: a simple API over a complex subsystem.

Observer / pub-sub: event emitters, signals, store subscriptions. Decorator: wrap an object or function to add behaviour with the same interface (retry, caching, logging wrappers, HOCs). Chain of responsibility: a request passes through handlers that may act or stop it (Express/Koa middleware).

Repository: hides data access behind collection-like methods. Factory: centralises object creation. Singleton: one instance (use sparingly; it is global state, and in Node a module export is already a singleton per process).
why: Shared vocabulary makes design discussions and code reviews fast: "wrap the SMS provider in an adapter" says a lot in five words.
trade: Pattern-itis: applying patterns where a plain function would do. Patterns should fall out of a real problem.

myth.m: Good code uses many design patterns.
myth.r: Good code solves the problem simply. Patterns are a means, not a score.

Adapter behind your own SmsSender interface
Observer

plain:
Design patterns are named solutions to problems that come up again and again. Knowing a few lets you recognise situations quickly and discuss designs in a few words.

A handful matter most in web development: Adapter, Strategy, Facade, Observer, Decorator (middleware) and Repository.
bridge: You already use them: Express middleware is Chain of Responsibility (each handler calls next() or stops), addEventListener is Observer, a HOC or a withRetry(fn) wrapper is Decorator, and a custom hook wrapping a messy API is a Facade.

walk.title: Wrapping an SMS provider with an Adapter
steps: Your code calls the provider's SDK directly in 12 places: eskiz.send({ mobile_phone, message, from }).
You may switch providers next year, and tests should not send real SMS.
Define your own interface: SmsSender { send(to: string, text: string): Promise<void> }.
Write EskizSmsSender that adapts your interface to their SDK, and FakeSmsSender for tests that just records messages.
The 12 places now call sms.send(to, text). Switching providers later means writing one new adapter.

terms: Wraps something to fit the interface you want.
A simple interface over a complicated subsystem.
Subscribers get notified when something changes.
Hides data access behind collection-like methods.
insights: Wrap every third-party service you depend on heavily; it makes testing and switching cheap.
In TypeScript most patterns are “an interface plus a wrapper”. A function type like (to: string, text: string) => Promise<void> often replaces a whole class hierarchy.
Naming the pattern in a code review (“let's put an adapter here”) saves paragraphs of explanation.

prod.summary: In production the patterns that pay off are the ones at integration edges: Adapter around every vendor SDK, Decorator for retries/caching/metrics, Strategy for business variants. The common failures are not “missing patterns” but patterns that hide errors (a decorator that swallows exceptions) or global state (singletons that leak between tests and tenants).
checklist: Is every heavily used vendor SDK (payments, SMS, storage, LLM) behind your own interface, with vendor types not leaking past the adapter?
Does the adapter translate vendor errors into your own error types (e.g. SmsRateLimited) instead of passing raw SDK exceptions up?
Do retry/caching decorators keep the same interface and re-throw after the last attempt? A decorator must never turn an error into a silent undefined.
Do retry decorators only retry idempotent operations (or send an idempotency key)? Retrying a charge without one can double-charge.
Are observers/event listeners removed when their owner dies? Check for MaxListenersExceededWarning and growing heap.
Is there a singleton holding mutable state? It will leak between tests and, in multi-tenant servers, between customers.
numbers: The “Gang of Four” book (Gamma, Helm, Johnson, Vlissides, 1994) catalogues 23 patterns in three groups: creational, structural and behavioural.
Node.js EventEmitter prints MaxListenersExceededWarning when more than 10 listeners are added for one event (the default defaultMaxListeners).
failures: Node logs MaxListenersExceededWarning: Possible EventEmitter memory leak detected. 11 message listeners added and memory grows.
An observer is subscribed per request or per component mount and never removed. Fix: call off/removeListener or use an AbortSignal in cleanup; do not just raise the limit.
Customers are charged twice when the payment API is slow.

A generic withRetry decorator retried a non-idempotent POST /charges after a timeout, though the first call had succeeded. Fix: send an idempotency key with each charge, and retry only idempotent calls.
Orders silently have no confirmation SMS; no errors in logs.
The SMS adapter caught every exception and returned undefined. Fix: map vendor errors to typed errors and throw; log and alert in one place above the adapter.
Tests pass alone but fail when run together.
A singleton cache or config object keeps state between tests. Fix: create instances per test via a factory and inject them; reset modules only as a last resort.

code.title: Adapter plus Decorator around an SMS vendor
code.note: The decorator retries only a known-safe error and re-throws everything else. A timeout is not retried here, because the SMS may already have been sent.

qs.s: You need to add caching, metrics and retries to a PriceApi client without changing its callers. Which pattern fits, and why?
o: Singleton, so there is one shared cache
Decorator: wrap the client in objects that implement the same PriceApi interface and add one behaviour each
Observer, so callers subscribe to price changes
Factory, so callers create different clients
qs.e: Decorators keep the interface identical, so callers do not change, and each concern stays in its own small wrapper that you can stack. Singleton is about instance count, not added behaviour.

qs.s: Your shop has three discount rules (student, bulk, promo code) chosen at runtime, and marketing adds a new one every month. Which design keeps the checkout code stable?
o: Adapter around each discount
A Facade over the checkout module
A Singleton DiscountManager with a big if chain
Strategy: each rule implements DiscountRule, and checkout picks one (or a list) by key
qs.e: Strategy is for interchangeable algorithms behind one interface. Adapter converts one interface into another; there is nothing foreign to adapt here. The if chain grows forever and every change risks the others.

qs.s: Code review: class Db { static instance = new Db(process.env.DATABASE_URL!) } is imported everywhere. Tests use one shared database and fail randomly in parallel. What is the most practical fix?
o: Add --runInBand forever
Make instance lazily created
Create the DB client in the composition root and inject it, so each test (or worker) can pass its own instance
Add a reset() method to the singleton
qs.e: The problem is global state that tests cannot control. Lazy creation still gives one global. reset() and serial runs hide the symptom and make the suite slow; injection lets each test worker use its own schema or container.

qs.s: This caching decorator wraps the price API. During a vendor outage, what do customers see, and which line is the most dangerous?

code.title: withCache.ts

o: return hit?.value ?? 0: products with no cached price get a price of 0 and can be bought for free. Re-throw when there is no cached value, and return a stale value only when one exists (and log it)
The cache never expires, so prices are stale forever
The Map grows without limit and crashes the process first
The decorator changes the interface, so callers break
qs.e: A decorator must not turn an error into a believable wrong value. Here a failure becomes the price 0, which looks valid to every caller. The TTL check does expire entries. Unbounded growth is a real but slower problem (bounded by the number of SKUs). The interface is unchanged, which is the point of the pattern.

qs.s: After an order is placed, orderEvents.emit('placed', order) (a Node EventEmitter) triggers the confirmation email, analytics and loyalty points. What is the main production risk of this Observer setup?
o: Listeners run in random order, so points may be awarded before the email is sent
After 10 listeners, further events are dropped

Listeners run synchronously inside emit: a throwing listener throws into the order code, an async listener's rejection becomes an unhandled rejection, and everything is lost if the process dies, since events live only in memory
There is no risk; this is the standard way to decouple side effects
qs.e: EventEmitter calls listeners synchronously, in the order they were added. It does not await promises. The limit of 10 only prints MaxListenersExceededWarning; nothing is dropped. In-process events are fine for UI-style notifications, but side effects that must happen (points, emails) need a durable queue or an outbox.

qs.s: Express middleware is a Chain of Responsibility. Read the setup. Which admin routes require an admin user?

code.title: app.ts

o: Both, because app.use('/admin', ...) applies to every /admin route
Only POST /admin/users/:id/ban; GET /admin/stats is matched and answered before the request reaches requireAdmin
Neither, because requireAdmin must be passed to each route
Only GET /admin/stats
qs.e: Express runs handlers in registration order. getStats is earlier in the chain and sends the response, so the auth step never runs for it. Put guards before the routes they protect, or attach them to a router (adminRouter.use(requireAdmin)) so order cannot go wrong.

qs.s: In Next.js development, after many file edits, logs show more and more database connections and Prisma warns about too many client instances. The code is export const prisma = new PrismaClient() in lib/db.ts. Why, and what is the usual fix?
o: It is a Prisma bug; downgrade Prisma
Create a new PrismaClient per request instead
Node modules are never singletons, so every import creates a new client
Hot reload re-runs changed modules, so each reload creates a new client while old ones stay connected; in development, keep the instance on globalThis and reuse it
qs.e: A module export is a singleton per module instance, and hot module replacement creates new module instances. Prisma's own docs recommend the globalThis pattern for Next.js dev. One client per request is the worst option for connections. In production, without hot reload, the module singleton works as expected.

interview.q: Which design patterns do you actually use every week? Show where they appear in a typical Node and React app.
answer: Adapter: every vendor SDK (payments, SMS, storage, LLM) behind our own interface, with vendor errors mapped to our error types.
Decorator: retries, caching, metrics and logging wrappers with the same interface; HOCs and withX(fn) helpers.
Strategy: business variants like discount rules or shipping calculators selected by key.
Observer: event emitters, store subscriptions, signals; plus the cleanup they require.
Chain of responsibility: Express/Koa/Next middleware. Repository and Facade around data access and complex subsystems.
A strong answer names the problem each one solved, not just the pattern.
followups: Which pattern have you seen cause bugs?
How do hooks replace some classic patterns in React?

interview.q: Design a retry decorator for outgoing HTTP calls. What can go wrong?
answer: Retry only safe cases: idempotent requests (GET, PUT) or requests with an idempotency key; never blindly retry a POST that charges money.
Retry only retryable errors: 429, 502/503/504, connection resets and timeouts; never 400/401/404.
Exponential backoff with jitter, honour Retry-After, a per-attempt timeout and an overall deadline.
Retry in one layer only: 3 retries in the client, the service and the gateway is up to 27 calls per user action (retry amplification) during an outage.
Expose metrics (attempts, final failures) and re-throw the last error; never return a default value.
followups: How would a circuit breaker work together with this?
How do you test the backoff without slow tests?

interview.q: When does applying a design pattern make code worse?
answer: When there is only one variant: a strategy interface, a registry and a factory for one implementation is just indirection.
When the pattern hides control flow: deep decorator stacks or event chains make “what happens on checkout?” hard to answer.
When it introduces global state: a Singleton holding mutable data leaks between tests and tenants.
When it fights the language: Java-style class hierarchies in TypeScript where a function or a union type would do.
Rule: the pattern should be the simplest fix for a concrete, current problem.
followups: How do you push back in review on pattern overuse without sounding negative?
Which pattern do you think is overused most in frontend code?

one: Ways to keep business logic independent of frameworks, databases and delivery mechanisms by making dependencies point inward.
an: The engine of a car does not depend on the colour of the seats. You can swap seats, radio and paint without touching the engine.
how: Layered: controllers → services → repositories → DB. Simple and common; risk of logic leaking into controllers or the ORM.
Hexagonal (ports & adapters): the core defines ports (interfaces like OrderRepository, PaymentGateway). Adapters implement them (Postgres, Stripe, HTTP controllers, CLI, queue consumers).
Clean architecture: entities and use cases in the centre; frameworks and DB at the edge; source dependencies point inward only.
Core logic becomes testable without a database or HTTP server.
why: Long-lived products outlast their frameworks. Keeping rules separate makes rewrites of the edges survivable and tests fast.
trade: Ceremony: interfaces, mappers and DTOs for a CRUD app add friction with little payoff. Use the full shape where domain logic is rich.

myth.m: Clean architecture means many folders named after layers.
myth.r: It is about dependency direction. Folder names prove nothing.

q.s: In hexagonal architecture, which depends on which?
o: Core depends on the Postgres adapter
The Postgres adapter implements a port defined by the core; the core knows nothing about Postgres
They are independent
The HTTP controller defines the port
q.e: Dependencies point inward toward the domain.

more: Vertical slice architecture as an alternative
lab: Implement one use case ("place order") as a pure function that takes ports (orders, payments, clock) and returns a result. Write tests with in-memory adapters. Then write the Postgres and HTTP adapters.
docs: Robert C. Martin: The Clean Architecture

plain:
These architectures share one idea: keep your business rules in the centre, independent of frameworks, databases and web servers. Outer parts (HTTP controllers, database code) depend on the centre, never the other way round.

In hexagonal terms: the centre defines ports (interfaces it needs, like “save an order”), and adapters implement them (Postgres, an HTTP API, a test fake).
bridge: It is like keeping your business logic in plain TypeScript functions and hooks, separate from components, so you can test the logic without rendering anything and swap the UI library later.

walk.title: One use case, three adapters
steps: Core use case placeOrder(cart, ports) checks stock rules, calculates totals, and calls ports.orders.save() and ports.payments.charge().
It knows nothing about Express, Postgres or Stripe; only the port interfaces.
HTTP adapter: an Express route parses the request and calls placeOrder.
Postgres adapter implements orders.save(); a Stripe adapter implements payments.charge().
Tests call placeOrder with in-memory fakes: fast, no database, and they test the real rules.

terms: An implementation of a port for a specific technology.
Which part knows about which; here, always inward.
insights: Start with one rich use case (checkout, pricing) in this shape and keep the rest of the app simple. The structure can grow where it pays.
Ports should speak business language (orders.save(order)), not database language (insertRow(table, values)). Otherwise the database leaks back into the core through the interface.
Vertical slices (one folder per use case, from route to SQL) are a lighter alternative when most features are CRUD.

prod.summary: In production the value of ports and adapters is boring and measurable: core rules tested in milliseconds without a database, and vendors swapped without touching use cases. The usual failure is erosion: one convenient ORM import into the core per sprint, until the “clean” core needs Postgres to run. Seniors enforce the dependency rule with a tool, and keep CRUD screens simple.
checklist: Does anything in core/ import from adapters/, an ORM, an HTTP framework or a vendor SDK? Block it in CI (dependency-cruiser or ESLint import/no-restricted-paths).
Do ORM entities or HTTP request types leak into use cases? Map at the edge to plain domain types.
Are transactions controlled by the use case (via a port like UnitOfWork) rather than started deep inside a repository method?
Is input validated at the edge (shape, types) AND invariants enforced in the core (business rules)? They are different checks.
Can the core test suite run with no Docker, no network and no env vars? It should finish in seconds.
Is the full layering used only where rules are rich? A settings CRUD screen does not need a use case, port, adapter and three mappers.
numbers: Alistair Cockburn published “Hexagonal Architecture” (ports and adapters) in 2005; Robert C. Martin's “The Clean Architecture” post is from August 2012.
Use-case tests with in-memory adapters typically run in single-digit milliseconds each, versus tens to hundreds of milliseconds for a test that hits a real database.
failures: Unit tests for pricing suddenly need DATABASE_URL and fail in CI with ECONNREFUSED 127.0.0.1:5432.
Someone imported the Prisma client into a core module “just for one query”. Fix: add a port method, implement it in the adapter, and add a CI rule that forbids core → adapters and ORM imports.
A change to the REST response shape breaks business rules.

Use cases accept and return HTTP DTOs directly, so the transport format became the domain model. Fix: the controller maps request to a command and the result to a response; the core owns its own types.
Half an order is saved when payment fails.

Each repository method opens its own transaction, so the use case cannot make “save order + reserve stock” atomic. Fix: a UnitOfWork/transaction port controlled by the use case; for the external payment call, use an outbox or a saga, not one DB transaction.
Adding a field to a simple admin form needs edits in 7 files (DTO, mapper, entity, port, adapter, use case, controller).
Full ceremony applied to plain CRUD. Fix: let simple CRUD go straight from controller to a repository or query; keep the layered core for rich domains like pricing or billing.

code.title: A use case that depends only on ports
code.note: The import arrows go from adapters/ into core/, never back. The order is saved before charging and the idempotency key makes a retried charge safe.

qs.s: A use case in core/ needs to send a welcome email. A teammate writes import { Resend } from 'resend' inside it. What should the review suggest?
o: Fine, since Resend has good TypeScript types
Move the import into a utils/ folder and import that from the core
Define a Mailer port in the core; implement it with Resend in an adapter; inject it
Send the email from the database with a trigger
qs.e: The dependency rule says the core must not know vendors. Moving the import into utils/ keeps the same dependency, just one hop away. A port keeps the core testable and the vendor swappable.

qs.s: Where should “a booking cannot be shorter than 30 minutes” be checked in a hexagonal app with a REST API, a Telegram bot and an admin CLI as entry points?
o: In the core (domain or use case), so all three adapters get the same rule
In each HTTP/Telegram/CLI adapter's validation schema
Only in the frontend form
In a database CHECK constraint only
qs.e: Business rules belong in the core so every entry point enforces them. Adapters validate shape (is it a date?), not policy. A DB constraint is a good extra safety net but gives poor error messages and cannot express every rule.

qs.s: A startup's internal admin tool is 90% list/edit screens over tables, with almost no business rules. The lead proposes full clean architecture with ports, mappers and use cases for every screen. Best response?
o: Agree; consistency matters more than effort
Use microservices instead
Remove all tests to move faster
Use simple controller-to-repository code for CRUD, and introduce the ports-and-adapters core only for the few areas with real rules
qs.e: The architecture's payoff is testable, isolated business rules. With no rules, it is ceremony. Mixing styles per module (or vertical slices) is normal in real systems.

qs.s: This use case lives in core/. The team now wants a Telegram bot and a CLI to cancel bookings too. What breaks the dependency rule, and what is the cost?

code.title: core/use-cases/cancelBooking.ts

o: Nothing: import type is removed at compile time, so there is no dependency
Passing now is wrong; the core should call new Date() itself
The core takes an Express Request, so it depends on HTTP. The bot and CLI would have to fake an Express request. Take a plain command like { bookingId } instead
The repository should be imported as a concrete Postgres class
qs.e: Type-only imports disappear from the JavaScript, but the design still depends on Express: the use case's input is shaped by HTTP, and Express upgrades can break core types. The dependency rule is about knowledge, not just runtime imports. Injecting now is good practice.

qs.s: A “transfer money” use case must debit account A and credit account B. Each repository method currently runs its own query. How do you make this atomic while keeping the core free of database code?
o: Open a transaction inside each repository method
Call BEGIN from the HTTP controller through the ORM and pass the connection to the use case
Debit first, and if the credit fails, run a compensating update in a catch block

A unit-of-work port, for example uow.run(async (tx) => { await tx.accounts.debit(...); await tx.accounts.credit(...) }), implemented by an adapter that opens one DB transaction and gives repositories bound to it
qs.e: The use case decides what must be atomic; the adapter decides how. Per-method transactions cannot cover two calls. Starting the transaction in the controller leaks database details into the edge and the core. A catch compensation is not atomic: if the process dies between the two steps, money disappears.

qs.s: Two weeks after this code shipped, a developer adds @Column({ type: 'numeric', default: 0.18 }) internalMarginPct to OrderEntity for a finance report. What happens?

code.title: core/placeOrder.ts

o: The public API starts returning internalMarginPct to customers, because one ORM entity is used as the domain object and the HTTP response. Map to a domain type in the core and to a response DTO at the edge
Nothing: TypeORM leaves new columns out of JSON by default
Nothing: TypeScript would report the extra field
The migration fails because the core imports the entity
qs.e: When one type serves the database, the domain and the API, a change for one leaks into the others. Here it is a data leak. After the insert, TypeORM reads the column default back into the entity (RETURNING), and res.json() serialises every enumerable property; TypeScript is happy to send extra fields. Mapping at the edges is the “boring” cost that prevents this.

qs.s: A backend has controllers/, services/ and repositories/ folders with 60 features. Every feature change touches all three folders and three code owners. The lead proposes vertical slices. Which statement is accurate?
o: Vertical slices forbid any shared code between features
Vertical slices group handler, logic and data access per feature, so a change stays in one folder; inside a slice the dependency rule (logic does not import HTTP or SQL details) can still apply
Vertical slices mean each feature must become a microservice
Clean architecture requires layer folders, so vertical slices are incompatible with it
qs.e: Slices are about grouping by feature (high cohesion). The dependency rule is about direction and works inside each slice. Small shared modules (a Money type, auth helpers) are normal. Slices are a code layout, not a deployment decision.

interview.q: Explain hexagonal architecture using a system you built. What did it buy you, and what did it cost?
answer: The core holds use cases and rules and defines ports (interfaces) such as Orders, Payments, Clock.
Adapters implement them: Postgres, Stripe, HTTP controllers, queue consumers, CLI. Imports point from adapters into the core, never back.
Benefit: core tests run in milliseconds with in-memory fakes; a vendor or framework change touches one adapter.
Cost: mapping code, more files, and a learning curve; not worth it for plain CRUD.
Enforcement: a CI rule (dependency-cruiser or ESLint restricted paths) so the boundary does not erode one import at a time.
followups: How did you test the adapters themselves?
Where did the architecture leak in practice?

interview.q: In a ports-and-adapters app, where do validation, authorization and transactions belong?
answer: Shape validation (types, required fields, formats) at the edge, with a schema such as Zod; reject bad input before the core.
Business invariants (“booking at least 30 minutes”) in the core, so every entry point enforces them.
Authentication at the edge; authorization decisions that depend on business data (“only the owner can cancel”) in the use case, with the caller's identity passed in.
Transactions controlled by the use case through a unit-of-work port; the adapter implements it with a real DB transaction.
External calls (payments, email) are not inside the DB transaction; use an outbox or saga for consistency.
followups: How do you return errors from the core so each adapter can map them (HTTP 409, a bot message)?
Is a database constraint still useful if the core checks the rule?

interview.q: When would you not use clean or hexagonal architecture?
answer: CRUD-heavy apps with few rules: admin panels, simple settings screens. Controller to repository is enough.
Prototypes and short-lived tools where speed of learning matters more than long-term change cost.
Small teams where the extra mapping layers slow every change and nobody enforces the boundary anyway.
Mixed approach is normal: a rich core for billing or pricing, simple code elsewhere.
Signal to add it later: business rules duplicated across controllers, or tests that need a database to check pure logic.
followups: How would you introduce it into an existing messy service step by step?
How do you keep consistency if modules use different styles?
