one: Modelling software around the business domain, using the business's own language, and splitting large systems along bounded contexts.
an: "Customer" means one thing to sales (a lead with a budget) and another to shipping (an address and a parcel). DDD lets each department keep its own meaning instead of forcing one giant shared definition.
how: Ubiquitous language: code uses the same terms as domain experts (Booking, Settlement, not DataItem).

Bounded context: a boundary inside which a model is consistent. Billing's Customer and Support's Customer are different models, translated at the edges. These boundaries make good module or service boundaries.

Tactical patterns: entities (have an identity, like an order ID), value objects (immutable values like Money), aggregates (a cluster changed only through one root object, like Order with its lines) and domain events (facts like OrderPlaced).

Rule of thumb: one transaction changes one aggregate. Other aggregates and contexts react to a domain event a moment later. The event is often saved in an outbox table in the same transaction as the order, then a relay publishes it, so the order and its event are never half-written.
why: The hardest part of big systems is the model, not the tech. Good boundaries reduce coupling between teams and services.
trade: The tactical patterns are heavy for simple CRUD. The strategic ideas (language, bounded contexts) are valuable almost everywhere.

myth.m: DDD is a set of folder names: entities, repositories, aggregates.
myth.r: Its core is talking to domain experts and drawing boundaries. The patterns serve that.

q.s: A Product table has 80 columns because catalogue, pricing, warehouse and marketing all added fields. DDD diagnosis?
o: Add indexes
Several bounded contexts share one model; split per context with their own representations
Use NoSQL
Add a cache
q.e: Each context needs different facts about a product. One shared model couples all four teams.

more: Context mapping (anti-corruption layer, shared kernel, customer/supplier)
lab: Run a solo event-storming session for a domain you know (e.g. car-wash bookings): write domain events on sticky notes in time order, then circle clusters into bounded contexts.

plain:
Domain-driven design focuses on understanding the business deeply and making the code speak its language. Its most useful idea is the bounded context: the same word can mean different things in different parts of a business, so each part gets its own model.

Those boundaries are also good boundaries for modules, teams and services.
bridge: If your Product type has 80 optional fields because catalogue, pricing, warehouse and marketing all added their own, you are seeing what happens without bounded contexts.

walk.title: Untangling “Product”
steps: Catalogue cares about title, description, photos, category.
Pricing cares about base price, discounts, tax class.
Warehouse cares about weight, dimensions, stock per location.
Instead of one giant Product, each context has its own model linked by product ID, owned by its own module or team.
Now a warehouse change cannot break the catalogue page, and each model stays small and understandable.

terms: The business area the software serves.
Using the same terms in code as the business experts use.
A boundary inside which a model has one consistent meaning.
A cluster of objects changed together as one unit with its rules.
An immutable value defined by its content, like Money.
insights: Draw contexts around teams and data ownership first. Services can follow later, or never: a modular monolith with clear contexts gets most of the benefit.
Event storming (domain experts and developers putting business events on sticky notes along a wall) is the cheapest way to find contexts before writing code.
Do not share one ORM model across contexts to save time. That one shared class is how the 80-field Product comes back.

prod.summary: In production, DDD's payoff is mostly strategic: bounded contexts that match teams and data ownership, so a pricing change cannot break the warehouse. The tactical part that matters most is the aggregate as a consistency boundary: one transaction changes one aggregate, and anything else is updated by events. Seniors spot a missing boundary from an 80-column table or from a word that means three different things.
checklist: Is there a glossary per context, and does the code use those exact words? If the business says “booking” and the code says reservationItem, fix the name.
Does each bounded context own its tables? Other contexts get data by ID plus an API or events, not by joining across.
Does one transaction modify only one aggregate? Cross-aggregate updates should be eventual, via domain events and an outbox.
Are aggregates small? Loading an Order should not load every past invoice and message.
Are invariants (rules that must always be true) enforced inside the aggregate root methods, not in controllers?
Is there an anti-corruption layer translating a legacy or vendor model into your context's model at the boundary?
Are money and quantities value objects (Money with integer minor units and currency), not bare floats?
numbers: Eric Evans' book “Domain-Driven Design: Tackling Complexity in the Heart of Software” was published in 2003.
JavaScript: 0.1 + 0.2 === 0.30000000000000004; store money as integer minor units (tiyin, cents) or a decimal type, never as a float.
Postgres row-level conflicts on a hot aggregate show up as lock waits; check pg_stat_activity rows with wait_event_type = 'Lock'.
failures: A small change to the shipping fields broke the marketing export and the pricing page.
One shared Product model served several contexts. Fix: split into per-context models (catalogue, pricing, warehouse) linked by product ID; each owns its tables.
Checkout throughput collapses during sales; DB shows many sessions waiting on the same row.
The aggregate is too large (e.g. every order updates one Inventory row for the whole store). Fix: make the aggregate smaller (stock per SKU per warehouse) or reserve stock asynchronously.
Stock was decremented but the order was never created (or the opposite).

Two aggregates were changed in separate steps without a reliable link. Fix: change one aggregate per transaction, write a domain event to an outbox table in the same transaction, and let a consumer update the other.
Meetings go in circles because “active customer” means paid-this-month to finance and logged-in-this-week to product.
Two contexts use the same word with different meanings. Fix: name them separately per context (PayingCustomer, ActiveUser) and record the definitions in each context's glossary.

code.title: An aggregate root that protects its invariant
code.note: Lines can only change through Order methods, so the rules cannot be bypassed. The repository saves the order and its events (to an outbox) in one transaction.

qs.s: Placing an order must (1) save the order and (2) award loyalty points in a separate Loyalty context. A developer wraps both in one DB transaction across both modules' tables. What is the DDD-style alternative and why?
o: Save the order and an OrderPlaced event (outbox) in one transaction; Loyalty consumes the event and updates itself, accepting a short delay
Use a distributed two-phase commit across the modules
Merge Loyalty into the Order aggregate so one transaction covers both
Call Loyalty's API before saving the order
qs.e: One transaction should change one aggregate. Events keep the contexts independent while the outbox makes the event reliable. Merging the aggregates makes them large and couples two teams; calling Loyalty first can award points for an order that then fails.

qs.s: Your app integrates with an old ERP whose Client record mixes billing, shipping and tax fields with cryptic names (KNA1_STCD1). How should your Orders context use it?
o: Use the ERP field names in your code so everyone matches the ERP
Build an anti-corruption layer that translates ERP records into your own Customer model at the boundary
Copy the ERP database into yours nightly and query it directly
Ask the ERP team to rename their fields
qs.e: An anti-corruption layer stops a foreign model from leaking into yours. Using the ERP names spreads its design across your code; direct table access couples you to its schema.

qs.s: An Account aggregate contains all its Transactions (some accounts have 2 million). Every withdrawal loads the whole aggregate to check the balance. What is the best redesign?
o: Add a cache in front of the repository
Load transactions lazily with the ORM
Keep a balance on the Account aggregate, enforce “balance ≥ 0” there, and store transactions as separate records referenced by account ID
Move the balance check to the frontend
qs.e: The invariant only needs the balance, so the aggregate should only hold what the rule needs. Lazy loading still loads everything when the balance is computed; a cache adds staleness to a money rule.

qs.s: The Order aggregate checks its rules in addLine. A controller then does the second statement. What is the real problem, and the fix?

code.title: order.ts and a controller

o: Nothing; controllers are trusted code
The fields are public and mutable, so callers can bypass the root's rules. Make lines private and expose a read-only copy
Mark the field readonly lines: Line[]; that stops push
Move the quantity rule into a database CHECK constraint only
qs.e: An aggregate root protects invariants only if it is the only way to change its contents. TypeScript's readonly on a field blocks reassignment, not push; you would need ReadonlyArray and a private field. A DB constraint is a fine extra net but gives late, generic errors and cannot express the status rule.

qs.s: A team has found five bounded contexts in their product: Catalogue, Pricing, Ordering, Warehouse, Billing. A developer says: “So we need five microservices.” What is the best answer?
o: Not necessarily. A bounded context is a boundary of model and language. A modular monolith can hold several contexts as separate modules with their own tables; split into services when deployment, scaling or team needs justify it
Yes; each bounded context must be a separate deployable service
No; bounded contexts are only database schemas
Yes, and each must also have its own team
qs.e: Contexts are good candidates for service boundaries, but a service adds network failures, distributed data and operational cost. Many teams start with clear modules in one deployable and extract later. Contexts are about models and language, not only schemas, and team mapping helps but is not mandatory.

qs.s: What does this print, and what does it teach about value objects in JavaScript?

code.title: money-equality.ts

o: true, 1, because the fields are equal
false, 1, because Set compares fields
true, 2
false, 2. JavaScript compares objects by reference, so value objects need an equals() method, and Sets or Maps should be keyed by a primitive such as `${minor}:${currency}`
qs.e: A value object is equal by content in the domain, but JavaScript does not know that. Both === and Set use reference identity (SameValueZero), so two equal amounts are two different objects. Forgetting this causes duplicate entries and failed lookups.

qs.s: Ordering publishes OrderPlaced through an outbox with at-least-once delivery. Loyalty sometimes awards points twice for the same order. What is the correct fix?
o: Switch to a broker that guarantees exactly-once delivery
Turn off retries so no event is delivered twice
Make the consumer idempotent: record the processed event ID (or a unique key such as order_id for the award) in the same transaction as the points update, with a unique constraint
Remember processed event IDs in an in-memory cache
qs.e: With at-least-once delivery, duplicates are normal, so consumers must handle them. A unique constraint written in the same transaction makes the second attempt a no-op. “Exactly once” end to end still needs an idempotent consumer. No retries loses events, and an in-memory cache forgets on restart and is not shared between instances.

interview.q: How would you find the bounded contexts in an existing system?
answer: Listen for language: the same word with different meanings (“customer”, “active”) or different words for the same thing across teams.
Run an event-storming session with domain experts: domain events in time order, then cluster them by who cares about them.
Look at data and change patterns: tables written by several modules, models with dozens of optional fields, files that change together.
Check team structure and ownership; boundaries that cut across teams create constant coordination.
Start by drawing a context map of today's reality (including the messy parts), then decide which boundaries to strengthen first.
followups: How do you handle a shared concept like “Customer” that every context needs?
What is an anti-corruption layer and when do you need one?

interview.q: How do you decide what belongs in one aggregate?
answer: An aggregate is the set of data that must be consistent immediately, in one transaction, because of an invariant (“total equals sum of lines”, “balance never below zero”).
Keep it small: include only what the invariants need; reference other aggregates by ID.
One transaction changes one aggregate; other aggregates are updated by domain events, accepting short delays.
Watch contention: a huge aggregate (one inventory row for the whole store) becomes a lock hotspot under load.
Ask the business how stale data may be; many rules that seem immediate can be eventually consistent with a compensating action.
followups: How would you enforce a rule that spans two aggregates, such as a unique username?
How do you handle concurrent updates to the same aggregate (optimistic locking)?

interview.q: When is DDD overkill, and which parts of it would you still use?
answer: Overkill: CRUD apps, data pipelines, and products where the business logic is thin; aggregates, factories and repositories add ceremony there.
Still useful almost everywhere: ubiquitous language (code uses the business's words) and clear ownership of data per module.
Value objects such as Money and Email are cheap and prevent real bugs (floats for money, unvalidated strings).
Use the full tactical toolkit only in the core domain where the company competes (pricing, scheduling, billing).
A good answer distinguishes strategic DDD (boundaries, language) from tactical DDD (patterns).
followups: How do you get domain experts' time if they are busy?
How do you keep the glossary from going stale?

one: The future cost of shortcuts and outdated design. Sometimes taken on deliberately, like a loan, and paid back with interest.
an: A loan. Borrowing to launch on time can be smart. Never repaying means interest (slower features, more bugs) eventually eats the whole budget.
how: Kinds: deliberate ("ship now, refactor after launch"), accidental (we learned a better design), bit rot (outdated dependencies, drifted patterns).
Make it visible: a debt register with impact ("adds ~2 days to every checkout change"), not vague complaints.
Pay down continuously: boy-scout rule, refactor as part of features in that area, reserve a share of capacity, and tie big paydowns to business outcomes.
why: Leads must argue for paydown in business language. "The code is ugly" loses; "this costs us a week per release and caused two incidents" wins.
trade: Not all debt needs paying. Code that never changes can stay ugly. Prioritise debt in hot, frequently changed areas.

myth.m: We will do a big rewrite to clear all the debt.
myth.r: Big rewrites usually take far longer than planned while the old system keeps evolving. Incremental replacement (strangler fig) is safer.

q.s: How do you best convince a product manager to schedule debt work?
o: Say the code is bad
Show measured impact: lead time, incident count, or hours lost in that area, and the expected gain
Refuse new features
Do it secretly on weekends
q.e: Translate debt into cost and risk the business already cares about.

lab: Run a churn report for the last year: git log --since="12 months ago" --format= --name-only | grep -v '^$' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -20. Cross-check the top files with how painful they are. That intersection is where debt costs most.

plain: Technical debt is the extra future cost created by shortcuts or outdated design. Like a loan, it can be a smart choice (launch on time) as long as you pay it back. Unpaid, the “interest” grows: every feature in that area takes longer and breaks more often.
bridge: The component nobody wants to touch because changing it always breaks something, or the 2-year-old dependency stuck on an old major version: that is debt with interest.

walk.title: Getting debt work approved
steps: You think the checkout module needs a rewrite. Saying “the code is messy” gets you nowhere.
Measure: the last 6 checkout features took 2.5× longer than estimated; 4 of the last 10 incidents started there.
Use git history to show it is the most frequently changed and most bug-fixed area.
Propose a bounded plan: 3 weeks to refactor incrementally behind tests, expected to halve future checkout work.
The product manager now sees a business case: faster features and fewer incidents. It gets scheduled.

terms: Future cost from shortcuts or outdated design.
The ongoing extra effort the debt causes.
Code that changes often and is complex: where debt hurts most.
insights: Interest is paid by whoever touches the code next, often another team. That is why debt in shared modules needs a named owner.
The debt quadrant helps in review: “prudent and deliberate” debt is a business decision; “reckless” debt is a quality problem.
A rewrite resets the debt counter, but it also deletes years of bug fixes hidden in the old code.

prod.summary: In a real team, debt is managed like any other cost: written down, sized in hours or incidents, and paid where it hurts most (code that changes often and is hard to change). Seniors attach paydown to the feature work in that area, keep dependency upgrades continuous, and avoid big-bang rewrites.
checklist: Is every deliberate shortcut recorded at the moment it is taken (ticket + TODO(ticket-123)), with the expected cost and a trigger for paying it?
Is the debt in a hotspot? Combine churn (commits per file over 6–12 months) with complexity; ignore ugly code nobody touches.
Is the impact stated in business terms: extra days per feature, incidents caused, on-call pages, cloud cost?
Are dependencies upgraded continuously (Renovate/Dependabot with grouped minor/patch updates) so no runtime or framework falls a major version behind?
Is there a fixed share of capacity (many teams use 10–20%) or a rule like “leave the area better than you found it” in every feature PR?
Are runtimes inside their support window? Check Node.js and Postgres end-of-life dates before they become a security issue.
numbers: Stripe's “Developer Coefficient” survey (2018) reported developers spend about 13.5 hours/week on technical debt and about 3.8 hours/week on bad code, roughly 42% of the work week.

Node.js up to version 26: even-numbered releases become LTS about 6 months after release, then get 12 months of Active LTS and 18 months of Maintenance; odd-numbered releases are never LTS. Node.js 18 reached end of life on 30 April 2025, and Node.js 20 on 30 April 2026.

From Node.js 27, the schedule changes: one major release per year (Current in April, LTS in October), every release becomes LTS, and each line is supported for about 36 months including a 6-month alpha phase.
PostgreSQL supports each major version for 5 years after its first release.
failures: A critical CVE fix requires upgrading a framework, but the upgrade is three majors behind and takes 6 weeks.
Dependency drift accumulated silently. Fix: automated update PRs every week, grouped minor/patch updates, and a rule that majors are scheduled within a quarter of release.
Every checkout feature ships late and 4 of the last 10 incidents started in checkout/.

Debt sits in a hotspot that is changed constantly. Fix: put measured paydown (characterisation tests, then incremental refactor) into the next checkout features, not into a separate “cleanup sprint” that never comes.
A 9-month rewrite is still not live; the old system kept getting features and the new one keeps chasing it.
Big-bang rewrite. Fix: strangler fig: route one slice (e.g. one endpoint) to new code behind a proxy or flag, ship it, repeat; delete old code as each slice moves.
The debt backlog has 300 items and nobody reads it.
Debt recorded without impact or owner. Fix: keep only items with a cost estimate and an area owner, review the top 10 each quarter, close the rest.

code.title: Find debt hotspots: churn × size
code.src:
# commits per file in the last 12 months (TypeScript only)
git log --since="12 months ago" --format= --name-only -- '*.ts' '*.tsx' \
  | grep -v '^$' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn > /tmp/churn.txt

# join with current line counts: churn, lines, file
while read -r count file; do
  [ -f "$file" ] && printf '%s\t%s\t%s\n' "$count" "$(wc -l < "$file" | tr -d ' ')" "$file"
done < /tmp/churn.txt | sort -k1,1nr -k2,2nr | head -15
code.note: Files high on both columns are the hotspots. Line count is a rough proxy for complexity; a complexity tool is better, but this takes one minute.

qs.s: Hotspot report: legacy/xml-export.ts is 4,000 lines, very ugly, changed twice in two years. checkout/pricing.ts is 900 lines, changed 140 times this year, involved in 5 incidents. You have two weeks. Where do you spend them?
o: xml-export.ts, because it is the worst code
Split the time evenly
Rewrite both from scratch
pricing.ts, because debt costs interest only when code is changed, and it changes constantly
qs.e: Debt in code nobody touches costs almost nothing. The cost is paid on every change, so churn times pain is the guide. The ugliest file is the tempting wrong answer.

qs.s: Before a launch, the team decides to skip the outbox and publish events directly after the DB commit, knowing a crash can lose an event. Which part of Fowler's debt quadrant is this, and what should accompany it?
o: Reckless and inadvertent; it should not be allowed
Prudent and deliberate; record it with the risk (lost events on crash), a monitoring check, and a date or trigger to pay it
Prudent and inadvertent; nothing to do until it breaks
It is not debt because it works
qs.e: A conscious trade-off with known risk is prudent, deliberate debt. It is fine if it is written down with a payback trigger and some detection. “Inadvertent” means you did not know; here you did.

qs.s: Your service runs on Node.js 18, which reached end of life in April 2025. The upgrade is not urgent for features. How do you argue for it?
o: It no longer receives security fixes, so every new CVE in the runtime stays unpatched; plus newer LTS versions are supported for years and dependencies are dropping 18
Newer versions always make code faster
Engineers prefer new versions
Upgrading is free, so there is nothing to argue
qs.e: End of life means no more security patches, which is a business risk anyone understands. Performance gains are possible but not guaranteed, and “engineers prefer it” is not a business case.

qs.s: npm outdated prints this in a service that uses npm ci in CI. Why is pg still on 8.11.3 when 8.16.3 is allowed?

code.title: npm outdated
code.src:
Package  Current  Wanted  Latest  Location
pg       8.11.3   8.16.3  8.16.3  node_modules/pg
zod      3.22.4   3.25.76 4.1.12  node_modules/zod

package.json:  "pg": "^8.11.3",  "zod": "^3.22.4"

o: npm ci ignores the lockfile, so it should already have installed 8.16.3; the cache is broken
The caret ^ allows only patch updates, so 8.16.3 is not allowed
8.16.3 is a new major version
The lockfile pins 8.11.3. The range only says which versions are allowed; something must update the lockfile (npm update, Renovate or Dependabot) for the new version to be installed
qs.e: npm ci installs exactly what package-lock.json says, which is what you want in CI. “Wanted” is the highest version matching the range in package.json. Caret allows minor and patch updates for 1.x and above. Drift like this is invisible unless a bot opens update PRs.

qs.s: Billing changes take about 5 days each; the team ships 12 billing changes per quarter. A paydown costs 20 engineer-days and is expected to bring each change down to 3 days. Roughly when does it pay for itself?
o: Never; refactoring does not ship features
After about 2 years
After about 10 changes, so within one quarter (24 days saved per quarter against 20 spent)
Immediately, on the first change
qs.e: Saving 2 days on each of 12 changes is 24 days per quarter, so 20 days are recovered after 10 changes. Estimates are often optimistic; even if the gain is half, payback is about two quarters, which is still a strong case. This is the kind of number a product manager can compare with features.

qs.s: It is October 2026. You can fund two items from this debt register this quarter. Which two?

code.title: debt-register.md
code.src:
ID  Area     Description                              Changes/yr  Incidents  Fix
D1  reports  Raw SQL strings, no tests                 3           0          5d
D2  auth     Session check copy-pasted in 14 routes   40           2 (authz)  3d
D3  ui       Old class components                      6           0          15d
D4  infra    Runs on Node.js 20                        -           -          4d

o: D3 and D1, because they are the oldest and ugliest code
D2 and D4: D2 is hot code that has already caused authorization incidents, and Node.js 20 reached end of life in April 2026, so it gets no security fixes
D3 and D4, because modernising the UI and runtime together saves time
D1 and D2, because missing tests are always the top priority
qs.e: Prioritise by cost of interest and by risk: D2 changes 40 times a year and has caused security incidents; D4 is an unpatched runtime. D1 and D3 are ugly but rarely touched, so they cost little today. Old or ugly is not the same as expensive.

qs.s: The app has 180 feature flags. 120 of them have been at 100% for more than 6 months. A developer says they are harmless. What is the best response?
o: They are debt: each keeps a dead code path, doubles the cases to test and confuses readers. Give every flag an owner and an expiry date when it is created, alert on stale flags, and remove both the flag and the old path
Keep them all as kill switches; more switches are always safer
Flags cost nothing because the dead branch never runs
Move them all to a config file so they are out of the dashboard
qs.e: A long-lived release flag is code nobody runs but everybody must read and keep compiling. A few deliberate operational kill switches are fine, and that is why “keep them all as kill switches” is tempting, but 120 stale release flags are not kill switches. Moving them to a config file hides them without removing the cost.

interview.q: How do you decide which technical debt to pay down first?
answer: Look for interest, not ugliness: churn (how often code changes) multiplied by pain (incidents, lead time, review time).
Separate risk debt (end-of-life runtimes, known CVEs, missing auth checks) from productivity debt; risk usually goes first.
Prefer items with a clear, measurable gain and a small first step.
Pay down inside feature work in the same area when possible; it is the cheapest time.
Ignore or explicitly accept debt in stable code nobody touches.
followups: How do you measure “pain” if you have no metrics yet?
What do you do when the most painful debt needs a multi-month effort?

interview.q: How do you get product management to give time for technical debt?
answer: Speak in their units: days per feature, incidents, on-call pages, customer-visible bugs, security exposure, cloud cost.
Show evidence from data (git history, incident reports, cycle time), not opinions.
Offer a bounded plan with a payback estimate and a first slice that ships in weeks.
Agree on a standing allocation (often 10–20% of capacity) so small debt never needs a negotiation.
Report the result afterwards; delivering the promised gain builds trust for the next request.
followups: What if they still say no?
How do you stop debt time from being taken over by urgent features?

interview.q: Tell me about a time you had to choose between a rewrite and an incremental refactor. How did you decide?
answer: Default to incremental: the old system keeps getting features, so a long rewrite chases a moving target.
A rewrite can make sense for a small, well-understood component, or when the platform itself is dead (unsupported language or framework).
Use strangler fig: route one slice at a time to new code behind a proxy or flag, and delete old code as each slice moves.
Protect behaviour with characterisation tests and shadow comparison of old vs new on real traffic.
Define “done” as old code deleted, with an owner and a date, so you do not end up running two systems.
followups: How do you handle data migration in a strangler approach?
What metric tells you the migration is going badly?

one: Changing code structure without changing behaviour, in small verified steps; and strategies for safely changing code you do not understand.
an: Renovating a house while living in it: one room at a time, keeping water and power on throughout.
how: Safety net first: characterisation tests that pin current behaviour (even weird behaviour) before changing anything.
Small steps: rename, extract function, move, inline. Each step keeps tests green and is committed separately from behaviour changes.
Strangler fig: route a slice of functionality to new code behind an interface or proxy; grow it until the old system can be removed.
Branch by abstraction: introduce an interface over the old implementation, build the new one behind it, switch with a flag.
why: Most real work is changing existing systems. Seniors make big changes look boring and safe.
trade: Refactors mixed with feature changes in one PR are hard to review and risky to revert. Separate them.

myth.r: The healthiest teams refactor continuously as part of feature work in the area they are touching.

q.s: You must change pricing logic in an untested 2,000-line legacy file. First step?
o: Rewrite it from scratch
Write characterisation tests around current outputs, then refactor in small steps
Change it and test manually
Add comments
q.e: Pin behaviour first so you can tell intended changes from accidental ones.

more: The refactoring catalog (extract, inline, move, rename)
lab: Take a messy function (50+ lines). Write characterisation tests for its current outputs, then refactor in 5+ tiny commits, running tests after each.

plain:
Refactoring means improving the structure of code without changing what it does, in small safe steps, checking after each step that nothing broke.

With old code you do not understand, the first step is writing tests that record what it does today, even the strange parts. Then you can change it with a safety net.
bridge: Extracting a custom hook from a 400-line component, step by step, with the UI working after each step, is refactoring. Doing it in one giant change and hoping is not.

walk.title: Changing a scary legacy function
steps: A 1,200-line calculateShipping() has no tests. You must add a new rule.
Write characterisation tests: run it with 30 real inputs from production and assert today's outputs, whatever they are.
Refactor in small commits: extract functions, rename variables, remove dead branches. Tests stay green after each one.
Now the structure is clear. Add the new rule with a new test.
If a test breaks unexpectedly along the way, you just found behaviour you did not know about, before users did.

terms: A test that records current behaviour as it is.
Gradually routing functionality to new code until the old can be removed.
Putting an interface in front of old code to swap in new code behind it.
insights: Kent Beck: “Make the change easy (warning: this may be hard), then make the easy change.”
Use the IDE's automated refactorings (rename symbol, extract function, move file) before manual edits; they update every reference, and the diff is easy to check.
A characterisation test that pins a bug is fine. Fix the bug later as a separate, visible behaviour change.

prod.summary: In production, refactoring is a sequence of small, separately deployable steps behind tests, with behaviour changes kept out of the same PR. For larger moves (new payment module, new data model) seniors use branch by abstraction or strangler fig with a flag, compare old and new paths on real traffic, and only delete the old path once the numbers match.
checklist: Are there characterisation tests (or approval/snapshot tests of real outputs) covering the code before the first structural change?
Is the PR pure refactoring with no behaviour change? Say so in the title; reviewers then only check equivalence.
Are steps small enough to deploy independently? Long-lived refactor branches create painful merges.
For risky replacements, is the new path behind a flag and compared to the old one on real traffic (shadow or dark launch) before switching?
For database changes, is expand/contract (parallel change) used: add new column, dual-write, backfill, switch reads, then drop old?
Is there a clear deletion step for the old code, with an owner and a date? Unfinished migrations leave two systems to maintain.
numbers: Michael Feathers, “Working Effectively with Legacy Code” (2004), defines legacy code as code without tests.
Martin Fowler's “Refactoring”, 2nd edition (2018), rewrote its examples in JavaScript; its catalogue is online at refactoring.com/catalog.
Stryker (mutation testing) defaults: thresholds high 80, low 60, break null (the build never fails unless you set break).
failures: A “pure refactor” PR causes a pricing difference of 1 so'm on some orders.

The refactor changed rounding order (round each line vs round the total), and no test pinned that. Fix: characterisation tests with real production inputs, including edge cases like rounding, before refactoring.
Reverting a broken release also reverts two weeks of refactoring.
Refactor and feature were mixed in one PR. Fix: separate refactor commits/PRs, merged first; the feature PR then stays small and revertable alone.
Six months after the “new billing module” launch, both old and new code still run and bugs must be fixed twice.
The strangler migration stopped before deletion. Fix: track remaining routes on the old path as a metric, give the removal an owner and deadline, delete as each slice moves.
The shadow comparison of old vs new pricing shows a 0.3% mismatch rate.
Real inputs exercise cases tests missed. Fix: log mismatches with inputs, turn each into a test, fix, and switch traffic only when mismatches reach zero (or are explained).

code.title: Characterisation test + branch by abstraction with a shadow compare
code.note: Run with shadow on in production until shipping_mismatch logs stop, then flip useNew, then delete the legacy function and the flag.

qs.s: You need to rename the column users.name to full_name in a service with zero downtime and several app instances running. Which sequence is safe?
o: Rename the column and deploy the code in the same release
Add full_name; deploy code that writes both and reads name; backfill; deploy code that reads full_name; stop writing name; drop it later
Drop name first, then add full_name
Create a view named name and hope old instances work
qs.e: Expand/contract (parallel change) keeps old and new instances working during a rolling deploy. A direct rename breaks every old instance still running during the rollout.

qs.s: A characterisation test for calculateShipping() shows that orders of exactly 0 kg cost 15,000 so'm, which looks like a bug. You are in the middle of a refactor. What do you do?
o: Fix it now inside the refactor PR
Delete that test case
Change the test to expect 0
Keep the test asserting today's behaviour, finish the refactor, then fix the bug in a separate PR (after checking if anything depends on it)
qs.e: A refactor must not change behaviour; mixing in a fix makes the PR impossible to verify. The odd behaviour may also be relied upon. Fix it on its own, with its own test and review.

qs.s: A team replaces an old PHP checkout with a new Node service. Plan A: build the full new checkout for 8 months, then switch. Plan B: a proxy routes /checkout/promo to the new service first, then more routes over time. Why is B usually better?
o: Each slice reaches production early, gives real feedback, and can be rolled back alone; the old system shrinks instead of being chased
B needs no tests
B is faster to write in total
B avoids having a proxy
qs.e: Strangler fig reduces risk by delivering value and learning in small steps. It is not necessarily less total work, and it does use a proxy or router; the point is incremental, reversible progress.

qs.s: A PR titled “refactor: simplify total()” changes the function below. Is it a pure refactor?

code.title: total.ts (before and after)

o: No. Rounding moved from each line to the total, so results can differ. Two lines of price 3, qty 1: before 3 + 3 = 6, after round(6.72) = 7
Yes; it is the same arithmetic in a different order
Only tiny floating-point differences below 0.01 can appear
Yes, if the existing tests pass
qs.e: Rounding is not distributive: rounding each part and then adding is different from adding and then rounding. Passing tests only prove that no test covers the difference. That is why characterisation tests on real inputs come first, and why behaviour changes go in separate PRs.

qs.s: You want to change getUser(id) to getUser({ id, includeDeleted }). The function is in an internal npm package used by three other repositories. What is the safe sequence?
o: Change the signature and update all callers in one PR
Keep both versions forever to be safe
Change it and publish a patch version
Expand/contract: add the new form alongside the old one, mark the old one @deprecated, release a minor version, migrate the three repositories, then remove the old form in the next major version
qs.e: Parallel change keeps every consumer working while they migrate at their own pace. One PR only works when all callers are in the same repository and deploy together. A patch release with a breaking change breaks anyone with a caret range. Keeping both forever leaves debt; the contract step must happen.

qs.s: A strangler-fig migration uses this nginx config. Where does a request to /checkout/promo-codes go?

code.title: nginx.conf

o: To legacy_php, because /checkout is the closer match
To legacy_php, because a prefix location needs the exact path
To new_checkout: /checkout/promo is a prefix of /checkout/promo-codes, and nginx picks the longest matching prefix. Use location = /checkout/promo or /checkout/promo/
It returns 404, because no location matches exactly
qs.e: Prefix locations match by string prefix, not by path segment, and the longest match wins regardless of order in the file. So a route you did not mean to migrate moved to the new service. In strangler migrations, route with exact or segment-safe rules and check the routing table with real URLs.

qs.s: You write characterisation snapshot tests for a legacy buildInvoice(). They fail on every run because the output contains the current timestamp and a random invoice ID. What is the right move?
o: Run vitest -u before each test run
Control the sources of change: fake the clock (vi.setSystemTime) and inject or seed the ID generator, or replace those two fields with placeholders before snapshotting
Remove the timestamp and ID from the legacy code
Skip automated tests and check the output by hand
qs.e: Characterisation tests must be deterministic to be useful. Freezing time and IDs keeps the real logic under test. Updating snapshots on every run means the test checks nothing. Changing the legacy output is a behaviour change, which is exactly what you must not do before the safety net exists.

interview.q: You inherit a 5,000-line untested module and must change it next sprint. Walk me through your approach.
answer: Find the seams: where can I call this code and observe its output without the whole app? Add a seam (a parameter, an extracted function) if none exists.
Write characterisation tests using real inputs (sampled from logs or production data), including odd cases, and assert today's outputs.
Refactor only the part I need to change, in small commits, tests green after each one; keep refactor and behaviour change in separate PRs.
Make the actual change with a new test, behind a flag if the risk is high.
Leave the area better and leave notes (tests, a short README) so the next change is cheaper.
followups: What if the code has no seams at all (global state, static calls)?
How do you sample real inputs safely if they contain personal data?

interview.q: How do you rename a database column or change an API field with zero downtime?
answer: Expand: add the new column or field next to the old one; old code keeps working.
Dual-write (or a trigger) so both stay in sync; backfill existing rows in batches.
Switch reads to the new field once backfill is verified; deploy and watch.
Contract: stop writing the old field, then drop it in a later release once no running version uses it.
Every step must be safe with old and new app versions running at the same time during a rolling deploy.
followups: How would you backfill 200 million rows without locking the table?
What changes for a mobile client you cannot force to update?

interview.q: How do you review a large refactoring PR?
answer: Ask for it to be split: pure moves and renames first (mechanical, easy to check), then structural changes, then behaviour changes separately.
Check that the PR claims no behaviour change and that tests were not edited to make them pass.
Look for the risky equivalences: rounding, ordering, error handling, null handling, async timing.
Prefer tool-driven refactors (IDE rename, codemods) and review the script rather than every line.
For high-risk paths, ask for a shadow comparison or a flag so it can be turned off without a revert.
followups: What would make you block a refactor PR?
How do you avoid painful merge conflicts with a long refactor?

one: Mix test types by cost and confidence: many fast unit tests, a solid layer of integration tests, and a few end-to-end tests of critical flows.
an: Checking a car: test each part on the bench (unit), test assembled systems like brakes with wheels (integration), and take a few full test drives (end-to-end).
how: Unit: one function or component in isolation. Milliseconds. Pinpoints failures.

Integration: several real pieces together, e.g. API handler + real database in a container, or a component with its hooks and a mocked network. Highest value per test for most web apps (Kent C. Dodds' "testing trophy").
End-to-end: real browser against a deployed stack (Playwright, Cypress). Slow and flakier; reserve for money and login paths.
Test behaviour through public interfaces, not implementation details, so refactors do not break tests.
why: Leads set the strategy. Too few tests and every deploy is scary; the wrong tests and the suite is slow, flaky and blocks refactoring.
trade: Coverage percentage is a weak target. 90% coverage of trivial getters says less than good tests of the payment flow.

myth.m: 100% coverage means the code is correct.
myth.r: Coverage shows what ran, not what was checked. Mutation testing shows whether tests would catch a change.

q.s: A team's 2,000 unit tests all pass, yet bugs keep appearing where the API meets the database. What is missing?
o: More unit tests
Integration tests running handlers against a real (containerised) database
More E2E tests for every page
A coverage badge
q.e: Bugs live at the seams. Mocked unit tests cannot see them.

lab: For one feature, write one unit test, one integration test (API + real Postgres via Testcontainers), and one Playwright E2E test. Compare run time and what each one caught.
Run Stryker mutation testing on a small module and see which mutants survive.
docs: Martin Fowler (Ham Vocke): The practical test pyramid
Kent C. Dodds: The testing trophy

plain:
Different kinds of tests have different costs and catch different bugs. Unit tests check one small piece; very fast. Integration tests check several real pieces together (an API with a real database); slower, catch more real bugs. End-to-end tests drive a real browser through the whole app; slowest and most fragile.

A good strategy has many fast tests, a solid middle layer, and a few end-to-end tests on critical paths.
bridge: Vitest + Testing Library component tests are in the middle; Playwright tests are end-to-end. Testing Library's guiding principle, “The more your tests resemble the way your software is used, the more confidence they can give you”, applies to every layer.

walk.title: Testing a “place order” feature
steps: Unit: the total calculation (discounts, tax, rounding) with many edge cases. Milliseconds each.
Integration: POST /orders against a real Postgres in a container: saves rows, rejects bad input, enforces stock. A second or two each.
Component: the checkout form shows errors and disables submit correctly, with the network mocked.
End-to-end: one Playwright test: log in, add to cart, pay with a test card, see the confirmation.
When something breaks, the cheap tests usually say exactly where; the E2E test proves the whole path works.

terms: Tests one small piece in isolation.
Tests the whole system through the UI.
Which lines ran during tests (not whether they were checked).
insights: Bugs live at the seams between pieces; integration tests catch them, heavily mocked unit tests do not.
The right shape depends on the app: logic-heavy backends lean toward the pyramid, UI-heavy frontends toward the trophy, with more integration tests.
Every E2E test is a long-term maintenance cost. Add one only for a flow where a failure costs money or trust.

prod.summary: In production the test suite is judged by two numbers: how long CI takes and how often it lies (flaky failures, or green builds that ship bugs). Seniors keep most logic in fast unit tests, cover API + real database seams with integration tests in containers, keep E2E to the few flows that make money, and treat flaky tests as bugs with an owner.
checklist: Do integration tests run against the same database engine and major version as production (e.g. Postgres 17 in Testcontainers), not SQLite or a mock?
Do the money paths (sign-up, login, checkout, payment webhook) have at least one E2E test each, and does almost nothing else?
Is CI time for the PR pipeline under about 10 minutes? Shard Playwright/Vitest across workers before it grows past that.
Is every flaky test tracked (quarantined with a ticket and owner) rather than silently retried forever? Track retry rate in the Playwright report.
Do tests assert behaviour through public interfaces (HTTP response, rendered text, DB row), not internal calls?
Is coverage used to find untested risky code, not as a gate number? Consider mutation testing on core logic.
Is test data created per test (factories/builders, unique IDs, transaction rollback or fresh schema) so tests can run in parallel?
numbers: Vitest default testTimeout: 5,000 ms in Node (15,000 ms in browser mode).
Playwright defaults: test timeout 30,000 ms, expect timeout 5,000 ms, no action or navigation timeout, retries: 0.
Stryker mutation score thresholds default to high 80 / low 60, with no build failure unless break is set.
failures: Playwright: Test timeout of 30000ms exceeded on CI only, passes locally.

CI machines are slower and the test waits on a fixed waitForTimeout or a slow real third-party API. Fix: wait on a web-first assertion (await expect(locator).toBeVisible()), mock third parties at the network edge, and shard instead of raising timeouts.
All tests green, but production fails with column "full_name" does not exist.
Repositories were mocked in every test, so SQL never ran against a real schema. Fix: integration tests with real Postgres via Testcontainers running the actual migrations.
CI takes 45 minutes and developers merge without waiting.
Inverted pyramid: hundreds of E2E tests for things a unit or integration test could check. Fix: push checks down a layer, keep E2E for critical journeys, shard what remains.
The same 12 tests fail randomly about 1 run in 20; the team re-runs CI until green.
Shared state between tests (same DB rows, fixed IDs, test order) or time dependence. Fix: unique data per test, fake timers for time, quarantine with an owner; never let retries hide it permanently.

qs.s: A team's suite: 40 unit tests, 30 integration tests, 600 Playwright E2E tests. CI takes 50 minutes and about 1 in 8 runs fails randomly. What is the first strategic change?
o: Add retries: 3 to Playwright
Buy bigger CI machines
Move checks down: test validation, formatting and permission rules with unit/integration tests, and keep E2E for a handful of critical journeys
Delete all E2E tests
qs.e: The suite is an inverted pyramid. Retries and hardware hide the cost but do not remove it. Deleting all E2E removes the only proof the full flow works; keep a few.

qs.s: A component test does await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 2000)) before checking that a toast appears. It is slow and sometimes still fails. Better approach?
o: Use await screen.findByText('Saved') (or Playwright's await expect(page.getByText('Saved')).toBeVisible()), which retries until the element appears or times out
Increase the wait to 5,000 ms
Check the component's internal state variable instead
Snapshot the whole DOM after 2 seconds
qs.e: Waiting on the actual condition is both faster and reliable. Fixed sleeps are always either too long or too short. Internal state checks couple the test to implementation.

qs.s: Coverage is 92%, yet a bug shipped where if (total >= 1_000_000) was mistakenly written as >, giving no free delivery at exactly 1,000,000. What tool would most directly have revealed the weak tests?
o: A higher coverage gate (98%)
Mutation testing, which flips operators like >= to > and reports tests that still pass
More E2E tests
Static type checking
qs.e: The line was covered but no test checked the boundary. A mutation tool (e.g. Stryker) creates exactly that change and shows that no test kills it. More coverage of the same weak assertions would not help; types do not check values.

qs.s: This Playwright test passes locally and fails about 1 run in 10 on CI with a wrong total. What is the best fix?

code.title: promo.spec.ts

o: Raise the wait to waitForTimeout(3000)
Set retries: 2 in the Playwright config
Remove the sleep and use a web-first assertion: await expect(page.locator('[data-test=total]')).toHaveText(...), which retries until the text matches or the expect timeout (5 s by default) passes
Wait for page.waitForLoadState('networkidle') before reading the text
qs.e: textContent() reads the value once, at whatever moment the sleep ends. A web-first assertion waits for the expected state. Longer sleeps make the suite slower and still fail on a slow day; retries hide the problem. Playwright's docs discourage networkidle for testing because it is unreliable and does not mean the UI has updated.

qs.s: Your suite has 1,200 Playwright tests averaging 6 seconds each. Ignoring start-up overhead and uneven test lengths, what is the minimum number of parallel workers to finish in under 10 minutes?
qs.e: 1,200 × 6 s = 7,200 s of work; 7,200 / 600 s = 12 workers. In real CI you need more, because shards are uneven and each one pays for browser and app start-up. The other strategic lever is to move checks down so there are fewer E2E tests in the first place.

qs.s: In Kent C. Dodds' “testing trophy”, the bottom layer is static analysis. Which bug is cheapest to catch there?
o: A function is called with a string where a number is required, and an unused variable hides a typo; tsc --noEmit and ESLint report both on every save and in CI
The discount is wrong at exactly the boundary amount
The checkout button does nothing in Safari
The API returns 500 when the database is down
qs.e: Types and linting catch whole classes of mistakes with no test code at all. They cannot check values (boundary logic needs unit tests), browser behaviour (E2E) or failure handling with real dependencies (integration tests).

qs.s: Read the coverage report. What does it tell you?
o: 62.5% of the lines never ran
The coverage tool is broken: 100% lines and 62.5% branches is impossible
Only if statements count as branches, so ?? and ternaries are ignored
Every line ran, but some decision outcomes never happened (for example, the else side of a condition or the right side of ??) on the listed lines; those paths are untested
qs.e: Line coverage counts lines that ran at least once; branch coverage counts each possible outcome of each decision. One line like const d = total >= limit ? free : fee can run while only one outcome is ever tested. Open the HTML report to see which branches were never taken.

interview.q: You are starting a new web app with a small team. How do you design the test strategy?
answer: Static checks first: TypeScript strict mode, ESLint, in CI on every PR.
Unit tests for pure logic with many edge cases (pricing, permissions, date rules).
Integration tests as the main layer: API handlers against a real database in a container, running the real migrations; components with a mocked network (MSW).
A handful of E2E tests for the money and login paths, run on every PR or at least before deploy.
Targets: PR pipeline under about 10 minutes, flaky tests tracked and fixed, coverage used to find gaps rather than as a gate.
followups: Where do contract tests fit in?
What would you change when the team grows to 30 engineers?

interview.q: How do you deal with flaky tests in a large team?
answer: Treat a flaky test as a bug: track it, quarantine it with an owner and a deadline, never just add retries forever.
Measure: retry and flake rates per test from CI reports, so you fix the worst first.
Common causes: fixed sleeps, shared data between tests, test order, real time and timezones, real third-party calls, animations.
Fixes: web-first assertions, unique data per test, fake timers, network mocking at the edge, stable selectors.
Protect trust: if people learn to re-run until green, real failures get ignored too.
followups: Should quarantined tests still run?
How do you find which test leaves shared state behind?

interview.q: Is 100% code coverage a good target? What would you measure instead?
answer: Coverage shows what ran, not what was checked; 100% with weak assertions is false comfort.
Chasing the last percent produces tests of trivial code and tests coupled to implementation.
Use coverage to find untested risky code, and branch coverage rather than line coverage.
Mutation testing (Stryker) on core logic shows whether tests actually catch changes.
Outcome measures matter more: escaped defects, change failure rate, CI time, flake rate.
followups: How would you introduce mutation testing without making CI slow?
What coverage threshold, if any, would you put in CI?

one: Stand-ins for real dependencies in tests. Each type suits a different job, and over-mocking produces tests that prove nothing.
an: A stunt double for the dangerous scenes. Use one for the car crash, not for the dialogue.
how: Gerard Meszaros' five kinds: Dummy: passed but never used. Stub: returns canned answers (getUser → {id: 1}). Spy: a stub that also records how it was called, so you can check afterwards (Jest/Vitest spyOn can also wrap the real function). Mock: set up with expectations of the calls it should receive and fails if they are not met. Fake: a working lightweight implementation (in-memory repository).
Mock at system boundaries you do not own: third-party HTTP APIs (with MSW or nock), time, randomness, email/SMS.
Prefer real implementations for your own code and for databases (Testcontainers, a test DB) when practical.
why: Tests full of mocks pass while production breaks, because they test your assumptions about dependencies rather than the real behaviour.
trade: Real dependencies are slower and need setup. Balance speed and fidelity per layer.

myth.m: Unit tests must mock every dependency.
myth.r: Over-mocking couples tests to implementation. If a refactor that keeps behaviour breaks 40 tests, the tests were checking the wrong thing.

q.s: A test mocks the repository and asserts repository.save was called with exact arguments. After a harmless refactor it fails. Better test?
o: More mocks
Use an in-memory fake or real test DB and assert the observable outcome (the saved record)
Delete the test
Snapshot test
q.e: Assert outcomes, not internal call sequences.

lab: Mock a third-party API with MSW in both tests and the browser during development.
Replace a mocked repository in some tests with an in-memory fake and see which tests become simpler.

plain:
Test doubles replace real dependencies in tests. A stub returns fixed answers. A mock also checks it was called in a certain way. A fake is a simple working version (like an in-memory database).

Use them for things you do not control (external APIs, time, email). For your own code and database, real versions usually make better tests.
bridge: vi.mock() and jest.fn() create mocks. MSW (Mock Service Worker) fakes the network so your components call a fake API that behaves like the real one.

walk.title: When mocks make tests useless
steps: A test mocks the repository and asserts repo.save was called with exact arguments.
You refactor to save in one batch instead of a loop. Behaviour is identical. 40 tests fail.
Meanwhile, a real bug (wrong column name in SQL) passed all tests, because the repository was always mocked.
Better: use a real test database (or an in-memory fake) and assert the outcome: “the order exists with status paid”.
Keep mocks for the payment provider and email service, which you do not own and cannot call in tests.

terms: A placeholder argument that is never used.
Records how it was called so the test can check afterwards.
Pre-programmed with expected calls; fails if they do not happen.
Mock Service Worker: a library that intercepts network requests in tests and the browser.
insights: Classicist style (real objects, check the result) vs mockist style (mock collaborators, check calls) is a real debate. Most web teams do best with classicist inside and mocks at the edges.
vi.mock('./sms') ties a test to a file path. Network-level mocks (MSW) sit at the real boundary, so they survive refactors.
A fixed clock is the cheapest determinism win: most “flaky” date tests pass once time is injected.

prod.summary: In real suites the danger is not missing mocks but mocks that drift from reality: the fake API returns a shape the real one stopped returning months ago, and tests stay green. Seniors mock only at the edges they do not own, intercept at the network level instead of mocking modules, fail on unexpected requests, and keep fakes honest by running the same contract tests against the fake and the real thing.
checklist: Are mocks limited to boundaries you do not own (vendor HTTP, email, SMS, time, randomness)? Your own modules and DB should mostly run for real.
Is MSW (or nock) set to fail on unhandled requests (onUnhandledRequest: 'error') so a test cannot silently hit the real internet? The default is only 'warn'.

Is mock state reset between tests in a way that matches how mocks are made? restoreMocks only restores vi.spyOn spies; vi.fn() return values set with mockReturnValue survive unless you use mockReset: true or create the mock inside each test.
Are fake response bodies built from recorded real responses or from the vendor's OpenAPI schema, not typed by hand from memory?
Does each in-memory fake pass the same test suite as the real adapter (a shared contract test)?
Do assertions check outcomes (returned value, stored row, sent message) rather than exact call sequences of internal collaborators?
Is time controlled with fake timers / vi.setSystemTime instead of real sleeps?
numbers: MSW server.listen() default onUnhandledRequest is 'warn': an unmatched request only prints a warning and is sent to the real network.

Vitest 5 defaults: clearMocks: true (call history is cleared before each test, implementations are kept), mockReset: false, restoreMocks: false. Vitest 4 and earlier defaulted clearMocks to false as well.
Meszaros' “xUnit Test Patterns” (2007) defines the five double types; Fowler's “Mocks Aren't Stubs” popularised them.
failures: Tests green, production logs TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'amount') from the payment webhook handler.

The hand-written mock still returns data.amount, but the vendor moved it to data.object.amount. Fix: build fixtures from recorded real payloads or the vendor schema; add a contract/schema check that runs against the sandbox nightly.
A test run sends a real SMS to a real customer number.
MSW was in default 'warn' mode and a new endpoint had no handler, so the request went out. Fix: server.listen({ onUnhandledRequest: 'error' }) and use sandbox credentials in test env.
Test passes alone, fails when the whole file runs.

A mockReturnValue or mockImplementation from an earlier test is still active. clearMocks clears only call history, and restoreMocks only undoes vi.spyOn. Fix: mockReset: true in config, or create mocks per test in beforeEach; avoid module-level mutable mocks.
A harmless refactor (batching inserts) breaks 40 tests.
Tests assert toHaveBeenCalledWith on an internal repository. Fix: use an in-memory fake or real DB and assert the resulting state.

code.title: Network-level stub with MSW that fails on unknown requests
code.note: The real fetch code runs; only the network is replaced. server.use overrides a handler for one test and resetHandlers removes it afterwards.

qs.s: You need a test that a welcome email is sent exactly once after sign-up. The mail goes through a vendor HTTP API. Which double is the right fit?
o: A real call to the vendor with a test address
A fake in-memory Postgres
A dummy mailer that ignores everything
A spy (or recording fake) Mailer that captures sent messages, then assert one message to that address
qs.e: Here the outgoing message IS the observable outcome, at a boundary you do not own, so recording it is correct. A dummy cannot verify anything; a real vendor call is slow, costs money and can fail for unrelated reasons.

qs.s: A team keeps an InMemoryOrderRepo fake for fast tests. Last month a bug shipped because the fake allowed duplicate order numbers while Postgres has a unique index. Best fix?
o: Stop using fakes everywhere
Run one shared repository contract test suite against both the fake and the real Postgres adapter, and add the uniqueness case to it
Add a comment to the fake
Mock the repository instead
qs.e: A fake is only useful if it behaves like the real thing. A shared contract suite catches drift such as missing constraints. Mocks would drift even more; dropping fakes loses fast tests.

qs.s: This test is flaky near midnight: expect(isToday(order.createdAt)).toBe(true) after creating an order. What is the cleanest fix?
o: Retry the test up to 3 times
Skip it in CI
Control time: use fake timers / vi.setSystemTime(new Date('2026-05-10T12:00:00Z')), or inject a clock
Use a longer timeout
qs.e: Time is a dependency. Fixing the clock makes the test deterministic. Retries and skipping hide the problem, and a timeout has nothing to do with the date changing.

qs.s: The project uses Vitest 5 with restoreMocks: true in its config. The second test passes alone but fails when the file runs in order. Why?

code.title: convert.test.ts

o: Tests in one file run in parallel by default, so they race

restoreMocks only restores spies created with vi.spyOn, and the default clearMocks clears call history but keeps implementations, so getRate still returns 12,650. Use mockReset: true or create getRate in beforeEach
restoreMocks resets every vi.fn() to return undefined, so the first test should fail, not the second
vi.fn() caches its first return value permanently
qs.e: In current Vitest, vi.restoreAllMocks() (what restoreMocks calls) only affects vi.spyOn. mockReset is the option that resets implementations. Tests inside one file run one after another unless marked concurrent. Many developers expect “restore” to reset everything, which is the trap.

qs.s: A use-case unit test must check the “payment declined” path: the order should end with status declined and no confirmation email. Which double fits the payment gateway best?
o: A dummy gateway that ignores all calls
A strict mock that fails unless charge is called with exact arguments in an exact order
A stub whose charge() returns 'declined'; then assert the order status and the recorded emails
A real call to the vendor's sandbox with a declined test card
qs.e: You need to control what the dependency answers, which is a stub's job, and then check outcomes. A dummy cannot return “declined”. A strict mock checks how you call the gateway, not what your code does with the answer, and breaks on harmless refactors. The sandbox is useful for a few integration tests, not for fast unit tests.

qs.s: Test B expects the name “Ali” but gets a 500 error, only when it runs after test A. What is wrong?

code.title: users.test.ts

o: server.use applies only to the next request, so test B should pass; the vendor URL is wrong
MSW resets runtime handlers automatically after each test, so the problem is elsewhere
Test B is calling the real vendor API
The 500 override from server.use stays active for later tests, because handlers are never reset. Add afterEach(() => server.resetHandlers())
qs.e: Handlers added with server.use stay until resetHandlers() is called. They apply only once if you pass { once: true }, which is why “applies only to the next request” sounds plausible. With onUnhandledRequest: 'error', a real network call would fail loudly instead of returning a 500.

qs.s: Your InMemoryProductRepo fake now has 300 lines that imitate Postgres full-text search, sorting and pagination, and it keeps drifting from the real results. What is the better approach?
o: Do not fake complex query behaviour. Test the real search adapter against Postgres (Testcontainers), and in use-case tests stub the search port with canned results
Keep improving the fake until it matches Postgres exactly
Use SQLite in memory instead, because it is also SQL
Mock the ORM's query builder calls
qs.e: Fakes are great for simple behaviour (save, find by ID). Query semantics like ranking and collation are exactly what a fake gets wrong. SQLite's full-text search and sorting rules differ from Postgres, so it drifts too. Mocking the query builder tests how you build a query, not whether it returns the right rows.

interview.q: Explain the difference between a mock, a stub and a fake, and when you use each.
answer: Stub: returns canned answers so you can drive a path (“payment declined”). Use it when you need to control inputs from a dependency.
Mock (or spy): records or expects calls. Use it when the call itself is the outcome at a boundary you do not own (an email was sent once).
Fake: a working lightweight implementation (in-memory repository, fake clock). Use it for fast tests with realistic behaviour, kept honest by a shared contract suite.
Avoid mocking your own internal collaborators; assert outcomes so refactors do not break tests.
At the network edge, prefer intercepting HTTP (MSW, nock) over mocking client modules, so your real client code runs.
followups: Which one do you use for time?
How do you stop fakes from drifting from the real implementation?

interview.q: How do you keep mocks of third-party APIs from drifting away from the real API?
answer: Build fixtures from recorded real responses or generate them from the vendor's OpenAPI schema, not from memory.
Validate mock responses against the schema in the test helper, so a hand-edited fixture that breaks the schema fails.
Run a small scheduled suite against the vendor's sandbox that checks the response shapes your code relies on.
Make unexpected requests fail (onUnhandledRequest: 'error'), so new endpoints cannot silently reach the real network.
Use a tolerant reader in production code: parse only the fields you need and validate them (for example with Zod) so drift fails loudly in one place.
followups: What do you do when the vendor has no sandbox?
Where does contract testing fit with third parties you do not control?

interview.q: Classicist or mockist testing: where do you stand, and why?
answer: Classicist (Detroit): use real objects where possible, doubles only for awkward dependencies; assert state and outcomes.
Mockist (London): isolate each class with mocks and check interactions; good for designing roles outside-in.
Classicist tests usually survive refactoring better; mockist tests can pin implementation and break on harmless changes.
Pragmatic stance: classicist inside my own code, doubles at the system edges (network, time, email), interaction checks only where the interaction is the requirement.
Name the cost honestly: classicist tests can fail in several places for one bug and may need more setup.
followups: How does this choice change for frontend component tests?
Have you seen a codebase where mocks hid a real production bug?
