one: Verifying that a provider API and its consumers agree on request and response shapes, without running everything together end to end.
an: Both sides sign the same delivery agreement and each checks themselves against it, rather than meeting in person every time.
how: Consumer-driven contracts (Pact): the consumer records what it expects; the provider's CI verifies it still satisfies all consumers' contracts before deploying.
Schema-first: an OpenAPI, GraphQL or protobuf schema is the contract; generated types and schema diff checks in CI catch breaking changes.
In a TypeScript monorepo, sharing types (or tRPC, or Zod schemas) gives compile-time contracts.
why: With several services or a separate mobile app, E2E environments become slow and flaky. Contracts catch breaking changes cheaply and early.
trade: Contract tools need buy-in from both teams. Schema diffing is a lighter starting point.

myth.m: Our E2E suite covers integration between services.
myth.r: It covers whatever paths it happens to run, slowly. Contracts check every consumer expectation on every provider build.

q.s: The backend removed a field the Android app used; nobody noticed until release. Cheapest guard?
o: Manual QA
A CI check that diffs the OpenAPI schema and fails on breaking changes (or consumer contracts)
More code review
A bigger staging
q.e: Automated breaking-change detection on the contract catches this on the PR.

lab: Add oasdiff breaking --fail-on ERR main.yaml pr.yaml to CI, comparing the OpenAPI spec on the PR against main. Make a breaking change and watch CI fail. (Without --fail-on, oasdiff only prints the changes and exits 0.)

plain:
A contract is the agreed shape of the requests and responses between an API and its clients. Contract testing checks automatically that both sides still follow it, without running the whole system together.

The simplest form: keep an API spec (OpenAPI) and fail CI when a change would break it.
bridge: Sharing TypeScript types between frontend and backend in a monorepo is a compile-time contract. Contract tests give similar protection when the client is a separate repo or a mobile app.

walk.title: Catching a breaking change in the PR
steps: The backend developer removes the field user.avatarUrl, thinking nobody uses it.
CI generates the new OpenAPI spec and runs oasdiff breaking --fail-on ERR against the spec on main.
oasdiff reports an error-level change: a response property was removed. The command exits with code 1, so CI fails.
The developer checks: the Android app uses it. They keep the field and mark it deprecated: true instead.
Without the check, the next Android release would have crashed on the profile screen.

terms: The agreed shape of an API's requests and responses.
The client of an API / the API itself.
Clients record what they expect; the provider verifies it (Pact).
Comparing two API specs to find breaking changes.
insights: Schema diffing in CI is the cheapest high-value check for any API with external clients.
A contract test checks the shape of the fields a consumer uses. It does not replace functional tests of the provider's logic.
Mobile apps make contracts critical: you cannot force users to update.

prod.summary: In production, contract testing is a deploy gate: a provider cannot ship a change that breaks a consumer version that is still live, and a consumer cannot ship code that expects something the deployed provider does not have. With mobile apps this matters most, because old versions stay installed for months. Seniors start with schema diffing in CI and add consumer-driven contracts (Pact) where several teams own both sides.
checklist: Is the OpenAPI/GraphQL/protobuf schema generated from code (or code from schema) so it cannot drift from what the server really does?
Does CI fail on breaking changes (oasdiff breaking --fail-on ERR, buf breaking for protobuf, GraphQL schema checks)?
Is there a deploy gate (Pact can-i-deploy --to-environment production) and is record-deployment called after each deploy so the broker knows what is live?
Do Pact provider states set up real data for each interaction, rather than one shared fixture?
Are removed fields deprecated first and removed only after usage of old clients drops (check logs or analytics by app version)?
For mobile, is there a minimum supported app version and a forced-update path for truly incompatible changes?
Do consumer contracts include only what the consumer actually uses? Over-specified contracts block harmless provider changes.
numbers: oasdiff breaking exits with code 0 unless you pass --fail-on ERR (or WARN/INFO); ERR means a definite breaking change, WARN a possible one.
Pact Broker: pact-broker can-i-deploy --pacticipant Web --version $GIT_SHA --to-environment production before deploy, record-deployment after.
failures: Android crash reports spike on the profile screen right after a backend deploy; the web app is fine.

The backend removed or renamed a field old app versions still read; web was redeployed together, mobile cannot be. Fix: breaking-change check on the schema in CI, deprecate before removal, and keep fields until old versions drop below an agreed share.
The schema-diff check is green but clients still break.

The OpenAPI file is hand-maintained and no longer matches the code. Fix: generate the spec from route definitions (e.g. Zod/TypeBox schemas) in CI, or validate real responses against the spec in integration tests.
Pact can-i-deploy fails with “no verification results” and blocks every deploy.

The provider never published verification results for the consumer's version, or the provider pipeline is not triggered by contract changes. Fix: publish verification from provider CI, use a webhook on contract_requiring_verification_published, and enable pending pacts for new contracts.
A harmless provider change (adding an optional enum value) breaks a consumer.

The client deserialises enums strictly and crashes on unknown values. Fix: clients must tolerate unknown fields and enum values (tolerant reader); the provider should treat new enum values in responses as potentially breaking for strict clients.

code.title: GitHub Actions: fail the PR on breaking OpenAPI changes
code.src:
name: api-contract
on: pull_request
jobs:
  breaking:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with: { fetch-depth: 0 }
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with: { node-version: 22 }
      - run: npm ci
      # spec generated from the route schemas, so it matches the code
      - run: npm run openapi:generate -- --out pr.yaml
      - run: |
          git show origin/${{ github.base_ref }}:openapi.yaml > base.yaml
      - name: Breaking change check
        run: |
          docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/w" -w /w tufin/oasdiff \
            breaking --fail-on ERR base.yaml pr.yaml
code.note: Without --fail-on ERR the step prints the breaking changes and still passes. The base spec here is the committed openapi.yaml on the target branch.

qs.s: A backend team adds a new required request field phone to POST /bookings. The web app is updated in the same release. Why might this still be a breaking change?
o: Older mobile app versions in users' hands still send requests without phone and will now get 400 errors
It is not breaking because the web app was updated
Adding fields is never breaking
Only if the database column is also required
qs.e: Adding a required request field breaks every client that does not send it. Adding an optional response field is usually safe, which is why “adding is never breaking” is the tempting wrong answer.

qs.s: Using Pact, the Orders consumer team publishes a new contract expecting GET /users/{id} to include loyaltyTier, which the provider does not return yet. What should happen?
o: The provider build fails immediately, blocking all provider work
The consumer deploys and handles the missing field at runtime
Pact automatically adds the field to the provider
With pending pacts, the provider build stays green while verification fails; can-i-deploy blocks the consumer until the provider ships the field
qs.e: Pending pacts stop a new consumer expectation from breaking the provider's build, while can-i-deploy still stops the consumer from shipping code that relies on something not yet live.

qs.s: A provider team asks why they cannot just rely on their big E2E staging environment instead of contract tests. Which is the strongest argument?
o: E2E tests are illegal for APIs
Staging tests one combination of versions, slowly and flakily; contracts check every live consumer version's expectations on each provider build, in seconds, without deploying everything together
Contract tests also test the UI
Contract tests replace unit tests
qs.e: The key gap in E2E is versions: production runs many client versions, staging runs one. Contracts are fast and versioned. They do not test UI or business logic, so they complement, not replace, other tests.

qs.s: This PR changes the User response schema used by the web app and by Android and iOS apps (Kotlin and Swift enums). Which change can break old mobile clients?

code.title: openapi.yaml diff (response schema)

o: Adding avatarUrl, because any new field breaks clients
Neither, because both changes only add things
Both equally
The new guest enum value: clients that decode role into a strict enum fail on a value they do not know. A new optional field is usually safe for clients that ignore unknown fields
qs.e: In responses, adding a field is safe for tolerant readers, but adding an enum value is a new possible value that old code has never seen. Strict decoders crash or drop the whole object. “Additive is always safe” is the trap. Agree with client teams that unknown enum values map to a fallback, and treat new response enum values as a change that needs a heads-up. oasdiff 1.33 agrees: it reports this as response-property-enum-value-added at error level, and does not flag the new optional field.

qs.s: Review this Pact consumer test. The consumer code only reads name. What is the main problem?

code.title: users.pact.test.ts

o: The contract is over-specified: it requires five fields with exact values, so provider verification fails on harmless changes or different test data. Include only the fields the consumer uses and use type matchers such as like()
There is no provider state
The test should call the real provider instead of the mock server
Pact requires every field of the response to be listed
qs.e: Without matchers, Pact compares literal values. A contract should describe what the consumer needs, not everything the provider returns today. The provider state is there (given), calling the real provider defeats the point of a consumer test, and Pact allows the provider to return extra fields.

qs.s: Consumer v2 (web) needs a new field loyaltyTier from the Users provider. Both teams use Pact with a broker, can-i-deploy and record-deployment. What is the safe deploy order?
o: Deploy the consumer first; it can show a loading state until the field exists

Deploy the provider with the field first; the consumer's can-i-deploy --to-environment production passes only once a provider version that verified the new contract is recorded as deployed in production
Deploy both at the same moment
The order does not matter when contract tests pass
qs.e: The new expectation must be satisfied by what is live before the consumer ships. can-i-deploy checks the verification matrix against what the broker knows is deployed, which is why record-deployment after each deploy matters. “At the same moment” does not exist in a rolling deploy.

qs.s: A protobuf change passes code review. What can go wrong, and what would buf breaking say?

code.title: order.proto (after the change)

o: Nothing, because protobuf matches fields by name
It only matters for JSON encoding, not for the binary format

Field number 2 is reused with a different type. Old services still read field 2 as the coupon string, so, depending on the library, they fail to decode the message or silently drop the value. buf reports the change on field 2; mark it reserved 2; reserved "coupon"; and give the new field a new number
The compiler rejects the file because numbers must be in order
qs.e: The protobuf binary format identifies fields by number and wire type, not by name, so field numbers are the contract. Reusing one changes the meaning for every client still on the old schema: in a test, protobuf-es threw “premature EOF” on the old bytes and protobufjs silently dropped the field. With buf's default FILE rules even a clean delete is reported (generated code loses the field); with WIRE_JSON rules the reserved version passes. The reserved statement prevents this mistake. Field order in the file does not matter.

interview.q: How do you prevent breaking API changes for a mobile app that users update slowly?
answer: Treat the schema (OpenAPI, GraphQL, protobuf) as the contract and generate it from code so it cannot drift.
Fail CI on breaking changes (oasdiff, buf breaking, GraphQL schema checks) with an explicit override process.
Deprecate first, measure usage by app version from logs or analytics, and remove only when old versions drop below an agreed share.
Clients are tolerant readers: ignore unknown fields, handle unknown enum values with a fallback.
Keep a minimum supported app version and a forced-update path for the rare change that cannot be made compatible.
followups: When would you create a new API version instead?
How do you handle a security fix that must break old clients?

interview.q: Consumer-driven contracts (Pact) or schema diffing: when would you choose each?
answer: Schema diffing: cheap, needs only the provider team, catches structural breaks (removed fields, new required inputs). Good default for public or mobile APIs.
Consumer-driven contracts: capture what each consumer actually uses, including example values and provider states. Good when several internal teams own both sides.
Pact adds a deploy gate (can-i-deploy) that knows which versions are live in each environment.
Costs of Pact: a broker, both teams' buy-in, provider-state setup, and pipeline webhooks.
Many teams use both: schema diff for every API, Pact for the critical internal integrations.
followups: How do you handle a consumer that you do not control, like a partner?
What are pending pacts for?

interview.q: What counts as a breaking API change? Give some less obvious examples.
answer: Obvious: removing or renaming a field, changing a type, adding a required request field, removing an endpoint.
Less obvious: adding an enum value to a response (strict clients), making a response field nullable, changing a default, changing error codes or the error body shape.
Behaviour changes with the same schema: different sorting, pagination limits, rounding, time zone, or rate limits.
Tightening validation: a field that accepted 500 characters now accepts 100.
Contracts catch the structural ones; behaviour changes need integration tests, changelogs and careful rollout.
followups: How would you change the pagination limit safely?
How do you communicate deprecations to API consumers?

sequenceDiagram
  participant Dev as Backend dev
  participant CI
  participant OD as oasdiff
  participant App as Android app
  Dev->>CI: PR removes user.avatarUrl
  CI->>CI: generate new OpenAPI spec
  CI->>OD: breaking --fail-on ERR (main vs PR)
  OD-->>CI: ERR: response property removed
  CI-->>Dev: exit code 1, PR blocked
  Dev->>CI: keep field, deprecated: true
  CI-->>Dev: green
  Note over App: installed versions keep working
diagrams.caption: What to notice: the break is caught in the PR, before any deploy. The Android app is never called; the spec comparison alone proves the change is unsafe.

diagrams.title: Consumer-driven contracts with a Pact Broker
diagrams.src:
sequenceDiagram
  participant C as Consumer CI
  participant B as Pact Broker
  participant P as Provider CI
  C->>B: publish pact (what the app expects)
  P->>B: fetch pacts of deployed consumers
  P->>P: replay them against the real provider
  P->>B: publish verification result
  C->>B: can-i-deploy --to-environment production
  B-->>C: yes, verified against the live provider
  C->>B: record-deployment
diagrams.caption: What to notice: the two sides never run together. The Broker matches each consumer's expectations with the provider version that is really deployed, and record-deployment keeps that knowledge current.
